content.title: Breaking the mould of traditional law firms
content.text:
From launching a new company to breaking the mould of traditional law firms Juliet Ralph has overcome imposter syndrome and created a groundbreaking law firm.

Juliet has had a very varied career, from working in pharmaceuticals to sales, and training. she even ran her own cake company ‘Shakey Cakey’ whilst her children were very young. “I love baking and it gave me the experience of setting up my own company and the highs and lows that brings,” she explained.

“What I didn’t fully appreciate was the foundations I was building for launching a bigger company.  We then reached a point where my husband Simon felt that he was at a crossroads in his own career. He was working in a large law firm and felt suffocated and wasn’t happy. He didn’t fit the traditional mould of law firms and wanted something more.”

Both were ready for a change and decided to launch their own law firm with its own values and culture. As Simon had previously changed roles, his clients made the decision to follow him. “He didn’t want to recreate what he had come from,” she continued “and whilst employment law isn’t ‘fun’ it shouldn’t stop you from enjoying your job.
“It has been a challenge effectively going up against such big names, but we stand out because we are different, colourful and fun.”
Juliet is now the CEO of Robinson Ralph and has proved you don’t have to be a lawyer to run a law firm. “Initially I used to apologise for not being a lawyer, but it is exactly that that makes me perfect for the role. Lawyers are great at law – that is what they do, but running a company requires a completely different skill set,” she added.

“I was conscious of this from the start and regularly felt like I had imposter syndrome. I could see the external perception of ‘what is she doing’, but I embody everything it takes to run a company. My focus for the firm is the marketing, the growth and providing different revenue streams. We don’t just give legal advice; we also offer training and practical tools to help businesses handle workplace issues with confidence.

“I am an early riser, and I start my day walking through the woods to school and gives me time without interruptions like phone calls and emails. This gives me focus for the day ahead, whether I am in the office or working from home. I still love baking and contribute cakes to a local community café nearby. It’s a small way for me to stay involved locally and do something I genuinely enjoy.

“The aim for our business is to continue growing and diversifying. We now have 8 members of staff and hope to reach ten by the end of this year. Simon and the lawyers focus on the law and clients, my role is pretty much everything else. We also want to build the additional services we offer such as the training and mediation.  With tribunal waiting lists reaching as long as 3 years before cases are heard, the more mediation we can do, will help to resolve cases before they reach tribunal and the court process.
“As the company grows, I would also like to step back and help other women in particular set up their own law firms.  I would do the hand holding and first few steps support, and based on my own experience, help them to avoid some of the mistakes I made along the way,” she concluded.

content.name: Featured Guest
content.title: Leeds Pride reveals full star-studded line up for 20th anniversary celebration
content.intro: Leeds Pride has unveiled the final line-up of performers for its landmark 20th anniversary celebration this summer, with more acts than ever before set to take to the stage across a fabulous two-day festival.
content.text:
Leeds Pride has unveiled the final line-up of performers for its landmark 20th anniversary celebration this summer, with more acts than ever before set to take to the stage across a fabulous two-day festival.
Headlining the weekend will be La Voix and Sweet Female Attitude. They’ll be joined by, Tomara Thomas, Livin’ Joy ft. Luzahnn, and Baga Chipz, alongside a whole host of other exciting names.
Presenting the festivities this year are Bradley Riches, Soraya Vivian, drag icons Mamma Bear and St Sordid Secret.
Taking place on Saturday 18 and Sunday 19 July, the milestone event will see the city come alive with its biggest and boldest Pride to date. Organisers are expecting record-breaking crowds for the packed programme of entertainment which will take place from 12pm – 10pm on both days.
The weekend promises to be the most diverse and inclusive in the festival’s history, with a major focus on supporting emerging and local talent across multiple stages.
In a new addition for 2026, Leeds Pride will host The Freedom Party, a ticketed Saturday event, helping to secure the future of the festival for years to come. Revellers can expect a high energy day featuring incredible stage shows and some of the UK’s best tribute acts, paying homage to the hit songs and pop icons of the last 20 years.
Tickets for The Freedom Party are available now from just £7.50, offering incredible value for a full day of live entertainment. Once inside, attendees can enter and exit the site freely throughout the day using their wristband.
This year also introduces a new and improved VIP area on Lower Briggate, alongside an expanded festival footprint, enhanced production and a wider range of experiences for visitors.
Alongside the main stage programme, a full schedule of fringe events will return, including the much-loved BIBIS Fundraising Ball on Friday July 3. Also returning for 2026 are the Drag Brunch Pride Special at Fibre, street parties, community-led performances and not forgetting the iconic Pride parade.
Festivalgoers can also expect a bustling event atmosphere with more food vendors and street food stalls than ever before, alongside local market traders, glitter artists, face painting, art, prints and more.
Jet2, the UK’s largest tour operator, returns as headline sponsor for the third consecutive year, and purchasers of the Leeds Pride wristbands can save £100 on a Jet2holiday as well as gain access to a range of exclusive perks and offers.
While Sunday remains free to attend, organisers are encouraging visitors
to show their support by purchasing Saturday tickets in advance.
A spokesperson for Leeds Pride said: ““Celebrating 20 years of Leeds Pride is a huge moment for the city and the community. This year’s line-up is our biggest ever, with more acts, more local talent and more to experience across the entire weekend.
“What we have in Leeds is genuinely rare, and that’s a Pride celebration that takes place right in the heart of the city. While many other Pride events are moving out to parks and greenfield sites, we’re proud to keep Leeds Pride woven into the fabric of the city. It creates an incredible atmosphere and means the celebration is shared across Leeds, supporting hotels, bars, restaurants and local businesses throughout the weekend.
“Pride remains as important as ever, and introducing a ticketed Saturday allows us to protect and grow the event for the future. We’re asking people to support us where they can, even a small contribution helps us continue delivering Pride for everyone.
“We can’t wait to welcome Leeds and visitors from across the UK to what will be an unforgettable weekend.”
Leeds Pride is still welcoming sponsors, parade entries and stall applications, with opportunities available for organisations and community groups to get involved.
content.quote: Leeds Pride has unveiled the final line-up of performers for its landmark 20th anniversary celebration this summer, with more acts than ever before set to take to the stage across a fabulous two-day festival.

content.title: Ward Hadaway strengthens Leeds corporate team with partner appointment
content.intro: Leeds law firm Ward Hadaway has appointed Alex Cooper as a corporate partner as it continues to build its corporate offering in Yorkshire.
content.text:
Leeds law firm Ward Hadaway has appointed Alex Cooper as a corporate partner as it continues to build its corporate offering in Yorkshire.
The appointment forms part of ongoing investment in the firm’s corporate team which was named the most active legal adviser in Yorkshire and the Humber last year.
Alex joins with more than 20 years’ experience in corporate transactional work, advising on UK and international mergers and acquisitions, disposals, investments and restructurings. This follows the recent addition of banking and finance specialist Aarti Parmar as a director in the Leeds corporate team.
Alex said: “I’m pleased to have joined the team at Ward Hadaway. Not only does it consistently top the lists of most active dealmakers in Yorkshire and the Humber, but the firm also punches well above its weight at a national level, and it’s exciting to be part of such a successful and ambitious business.
“We have genuine strength and depth in our team which will allow us to continue to deliver high quality outcomes for a diverse range of clients across the region.”
Nik Tunley, head of corporate said: “We have built a market-leading mid-market M&A and finance practice, recognised nationally for its expertise, credibility and consistent delivery of high-quality outcomes. Our focus remains on strengthening that reputation further, supported by the breadth and depth of capability we offer across our offices.
“The arrival of Alex and Aarti in Leeds significantly enhances the
scale and experience of our offering, enabling us to support clients through increasingly complex and high-value transactions. Their addition reinforces our commitment to a partner-led service, combining clear, pragmatic advice with the consistently high standards that define our M&A and finance practice.”
The firm has seen sustained levels of deal activity and was recently ranked among the UK’s most active legal advisers in 2025 in Experian MarketIQ’s latest UK and Republic of Ireland M&A Review.
Steven Petrie, managing partner said: “We have continued to invest in our corporate team over the past 12 months through senior appointments and have strengthened our already impressive corporate offering nationally.
“Alex brings significant experience in mid-market transactions and adds further depth to the team as we continue to grow, with more developments in the pipeline.”
content.quote: Leeds law firm Ward Hadaway has appointed Alex Cooper as a corporate partner as it continues to build its corporate offering in Yorkshire.

content.title: Looking for a revitalised and radiant finish for your skin?
content.intro: In the heart of Harrogate, Michelle Clarke, founder of HIFU Clinics Group, celebrates a decade of specialization in advanced HIFU skin tightening.
content.author: Debbie Dobson
content.text:
In the heart of Harrogate, Michelle Clarke, founder of HIFU Clinics Group, celebrates a decade of specialization in advanced HIFU skin tightening. Over the past ten years, Michelle has become a trusted expert, sought after by discerning clients, including fellow professionals and celebrities. Clients travel from across the UK to experience her multi-layered approach, which delivers natural, lasting results.

The journey starts with the Aura scanner, a clinical-grade device that creates a detailed digital map of the face and neck. This objective analysis ensures precise, customized treatment plans. Michelle’s philosophy is built on three pillars: Precision. Expertise. Transformation.

Her advanced method addresses the skin in layers. At deeper levels, HIFU stimulates collagen and elastin, lifting and firming the underlying structure. At intermediate depths, texture is refined, and fine lines softened. On the surface, the skin is revitalized for a radiant finish. This layered strategy ensures balanced and natural rejuvenation.

Clients consistently praise this approach, noting that results are subtle yet transformative. The Aura scanner is used not only at the start but also in follow-ups, offering clinical proof of progress.

Michelle’s expertise draws clients
from afar, from industry experts to high-profile individuals, all seeking the assurance of Precision. Expertise. Transformation. With over 10,000 procedures performed, her blend of science, technology, and artistry has set a standard in the field. At HIFU Clinics Group, clients embark on a journey of confidence—guided by the pillars of precise care, expert execution, and transformative results.

content.title: Law firm appoints family and matrimonial partner
content.intro: Ward Hadaway has appointed family lawyer Maria Coster as a partner, where she will lead the family and matrimonial team in the Leeds office, working closely with colleagues across the firm’s national team.
content.text:
Ward Hadaway has appointed family lawyer Maria Coster as a partner, where she will lead the family and matrimonial team in the Leeds office, working closely with colleagues across the firm’s national team.
Recognised by The Legal 500 as a Rising Star and Next Generation Partner, Maria has worked exclusively in family law for nearly 15 years, handling financial disputes and private children matters.
Her work includes divorce and dissolution, high-value financial cases involving business interests and arrangements concerning children. She also supports clients with asset protection, including pre- and post-nuptial and cohabitation agreements.
Maria said: “My focus is on leading the matrimonial team in Leeds, working alongside partner Andrea Dyer and managing associate Greg Cross, to build on the foundations already in place. That includes strengthening the group and broadening the range of work we handle.
“I have spent my career working on financial and children’s matters, often involving significant assets or challenging personal circumstances. Bringing that experience into this role will be important as we continue to deliver clear, practical advice.
“I am looking forward to working with colleagues across the firm, building on existing relationships and contributing to the continued development of the national family offering. Maintaining a consistent, high-quality service for clients will remain central to that.”
The appointment forms part of continued investment
in this area of the firm, with a focus on strengthening capability and supporting the long-term growth of the team.
Liz Bottrill, who heads up the national family and matrimonial department, said: “Maria adds further strength to our team, bringing extensive experience across family matters alongside a pragmatic approach to client advice.
“As we continue to invest in our people and in those working on complex and often sensitive situations, Maria’s expertise and leadership will play an important role.”
This appointment is the latest into the growing private client department, led by Alison Hall who herself joined in 2025. With new additions into the teams who provide family, contentious probate, and wills, estate planning and succession services, the department is growing in strength and reach, reinforcing the firm’s full-service reputation across clients’ professional and personal needs.
Managing partner Steven Petrie added: “We’re focused on building teams with the right mix of experience and leadership to support the firm’s long-term development.
“Maria brings both, with a strong track record in advising on complex matters and developing teams. Her appointment strengthens the Leeds office at a time of continued growth and adds further depth to our overall capability in our thriving private client services team.”
content.quote: Ward Hadaway has appointed family lawyer Maria Coster as a partner, where she will lead the family and matrimonial team in the Leeds office, working closely with colleagues across the firm’s national team.

content.name: Featured Guest
content.title: Hull College vice principal Awarded MBE in King’s Birthday Honours
content.quote: Hull College is celebrating after vice principal Governance & Compliance, Catherine Sykes, was awarded an MBE in His Majesty The King’s Birthday Honours List for her outstanding services to education.
content.text:
Hull College is celebrating after vice principal Governance & Compliance, Catherine Sykes, was awarded an MBE in His Majesty The King’s Birthday Honours List for her outstanding services to education.

The prestigious award recognises Catherine’s significant contribution to education over more than a decade, including her role in helping transform Hull College’s governance, her national leadership across the Further Education sector, and her commitment to supporting local communities and charitable causes across the region.

A highly respected governance professional, she has played a central role in Hull College’s transformation from a college in national intervention to an institution recognised for excellence, with governance now considered one of its greatest strengths. Beyond the college, Sykes serves as a National Leader of Governance for the Department for Education, supporting boards and governance professionals across England.

She has gained national recognition for pioneering the ethical use of artificial intelligence in governance, helping organisations modernise decision-making while maintaining transparency, accountability, and public trust.

Alongside her professional achievements, Catherine has dedicated significant time to supporting her local community. She serves as a Trustee of the HEY Smile Foundation, helping to improve opportunities and outcomes for communities across Hull and East Yorkshire, and is Chair of Friends of Newport School, supporting educational and community activities in her local area. She also leads and continues to support the delivery of the prestigious International Youth Championships at Bishop Burton College in association with British Eventing, creating opportunities for young people from around the UK to develop skills, confidence and lifelong friendships through sport.

Reacting to the news, Catherine said: “Receiving news of this honour was completely unexpected and incredibly humbling. I am both deeply honoured and immensely proud to be recognised in this way.

“Education has the power to transform lives, and I have been fortunate throughout my career to work alongside people who are passionate about creating opportunities for others. While this honour bears my
name, it reflects the collective efforts of so many people who have supported and inspired me along the way.

“From my colleagues at Hull College and across the Further Education sector to the communities and organisations I have had the privilege to serve, I am grateful for every opportunity to contribute. I remain passionate about championing excellence in governance, embracing innovation responsibly, and ensuring education continues to create opportunities for individuals and communities to thrive.”

Debra Gray CBE, chief executive and Principal of Hull College, said: “Everyone at Hull College is absolutely delighted that Catherine has received this richly deserved honour. Catherine is an exceptional leader whose expertise, professionalism, and unwavering commitment to education have had a profound impact, not only on Hull College but on the wider Further Education sector nationally.

“Her leadership has been instrumental in strengthening governance at Hull College and supporting our transformation journey. Catherine consistently demonstrates the highest standards of integrity, innovation, and public service, and this recognition is a fitting tribute to her outstanding contribution to the education sector and her wider community.”

A member of the Chartered Governance Institute and qualified to Master’s level in Corporate Governance, Catherine has become one of the most respected voices in governance within the education sector. She has been shortlisted nationally for Governance Professional of the Year and AI Leader of the Year, and continues to champion innovation, ethical leadership, and best practice across education and beyond.
Her appointment as an MBE recognises a career defined by service, leadership, and innovation, as well as an unwavering commitment to improving opportunities for learners, organisations, and communities across Hull, East Yorkshire, and
beyond.

content.title: What do you know about the capital of the county?
content.intro: Few cities in Britain can match York for the depth and continuity of its history.
pullQuotes: In 866 Viking forces captured the city and renamed it Jorvik
content.text:
Few cities in Britain can match York for the depth and continuity of its history. From Roman foundations to Viking rule and medieval prominence, York has played a central role in shaping the story of England.
York was founded in 71 CE by the Roman Ninth Legion and named Eboracum. Its strategic position at the confluence of the rivers Ouse and Foss, made it a vital military and administrative centre. Emperors such as Septimius Severus ruled from York and it was here that Constantine the Great was proclaimed emperor in 306 CE. Today, remains of Roman walls and roads still underpin parts of modern York as we know it today.

After the Romans withdrew in the early 5th century, York declined before re-emerging as an important Anglo-Saxon settlement. In 866 Viking forces captured the city and renamed it Jorvik. Under Norse rule, York became a thriving trade hub connecting England with Scandinavia and beyond.
Following the Norman conquest of 1066, York became the administrative centre of Northern England. The construction of York Minster, one of the largest gothic cathedrals in Europe, symbolised its religious importance. The city walls, much of which still stand today, were expanded during this period.

By the 16th and 17th centuries, York remained influential but began to lose economic ground to emerging industrial centres. During the English civil war, the city was a royalist stronghold and endured a significant siege in 1644.

Although York was not a major industrial powerhouse like neighbouring Manchester and Leeds, it adapted through industries such as railways and confectionery. Companies like Rowntree’s and Terry’s of York became nationally recognised brands. The arrival of the railway in the 19th century transformed York into a key transport hub, reinforcing its regional importance. Did you know that the building that now houses The Grand Hotel, just a short walk from the main station, was originally the headquarters of the railway in York and Queen Victoria famously stopped in York for tea whilst passing through on a train, at The Milner Hotel, situated within the train station complex.

York is famous as the UK’s original ‘chocolate city’ due to its rich 300-year history of cocoa manufacturing. This legacy was built by pioneering quaker families who revolutionised the industry, transforming chocolate from a luxury drink for the elite, into an affordable treat for the masses.  Some of the world’s most famous chocolate bars were invented in York. Rowntree’s introduced staples like the KitKat, Aero, Smarties, Quality Street and the Yorkie Bar. Terry’s is globally renowned for the Terry’s Chocolate Orange.

Today, York keeps its sweet heritage alive. The Nestle factory on Haxby Road still produces millions of KitKats daily and visitors can experience the city’s legacy firsthand by visiting the interactive York’s chocolate story museum or taking hands-on workshops at York Cocoa Works.
Modern York is celebrated for its heritage and tourism. Visitors are drawn to its preserved medieval streets like The Shambles, the city walls, its famous racecourse that hosts the annual Ebor festival and was the chosen racecourse by the late Queen replacing Royal Ascot, when Royal Ascot was being refurbished and the city’s museums. Today, the city balances historical preservation with a vibrant cultural life, making it one of England’s most distinctive destinations.

content.title: New partnership rounds up ‘shop local’ gifts for the end of term
pullQuotes: Delivered by Bradford BID, the Bradford Gift Card is a local gift card that can be spent with over 120 local businesses
content.text:
People can now group collect, fee-free, for the Bradford City Centre Gift Card. Business leaders say they hope the move will divert teacher gift spending into the local economy.

A new partnership between Bradford BID, Miconex, and GiftRound will simplify group collecting for the Bradford City Centre Gift Card in time for the end of the school year.
From now, people will be able to set up a group collection for the Bradford City Centre Gift Card www.bradfordgiftcard.com and redeem as a digital gift card, fee-free.

Once the GiftRound collection closes, the digital Bradford City Centre Gift Card can be sent directly to the organiser with a printable gift card, or directly to the recipient with a link to messages from the contributors. Collections can also be split across multiple gifts/recipients.

Delivered by Bradford BID, the Bradford Gift Card is a local gift card that can be spent with over 120 local businesses including big brands like Primark, J D Sports and Nandos, and local independent businesses like Pizza Pieces, The Alhambra and Blossoms.

The ability to group collect for a Bradford Gift Card arrives just in time for the end of term teacher gifting season. With an estimated 4.5m children in state funded primary schools in the UK and parents spending an average of £9.06 on teacher gifts, over £4m is spent on teacher gifts at the end of term, and again at Christmas, if just 10% of families buy a gift for a teacher.

The partnership between Miconex and GiftRound will enable group collecting for over 90+ Town & City Gift Card programmes in the UK. Miconex announced over £24m in local gift card sales across its network in 2025, a 60% increase on 2024 as shoppers make the move to local gift cards to show support for local businesses.

Group collecting platform GiftRound reports that the average contribution to a teacher gift on their platform is £10, with an average overall teacher collection value of £145. The tech firm was founded in 2018, giving people an easy, fee-free way to collect money for various occasions including leaving gifts, new babies, weddings and teacher gifts.
Over 175,000 collections have been created to date through GiftRound with over £9 million in gift cards/vouchers ordered through the platform.

Nikki Chadburn, business communications manager at Bradford BID said: “The Bradford City Centre Gift Card is popular for gifts, rewards and incentives, giving the recipient money to spend with over FF120 amazing
local businesses right here in Bradford city centre.The ability to group collect, gather messages in one place, and send our local gift card easily is a positive development and will be useful for end of term gifts but also wedding gifts, leaving gifts, new baby gifts and more. With over £4m being spent on teacher gifts at the end of term, the more spend we can lock into our economy through the Bradford City Centre Gift Card, the more businesses we can keep open and the more vibrant our city will be.”

Craig Forsythe, CEO & founder at GiftRound, said: “Going live with Town & City Gift Cards, including the Bradford City Centre Gift Card, across 90+ UK towns and cities is exciting. We’re making it easy to group collect for all kinds of occasions and redeem as a local gift card where the beneficiaries are the local businesses who power our economy. Gifts for teachers is one of our most popular collections and it makes huge sense. Instead of teachers receiving multiple mugs or gift sets, parents can each put a small amount into a collection, and the teacher receives the collection as a gift card to buy something they’d really like.”

David O’Neil, chief customer and growth officer at Miconex, said: “The Bradford Gift Card is the ultimate ‘shop local’ gift card, blending unbeatable local choice and unrivalled support for local. It’s fantastic to see this new technology go live in time for the end of term – helping people easily collect money as a group for a teacher’s gift – and gift a teacher the best of local in one gift card.”

content.title: Wakefield’s historic civic buildings to become thriving new heart for creativity and culture
content.intro: The project is being delivered by Yorkshire-based property investment and heritage specialists Rushbond, in partnership with Wakefield Council, as part of a wider programme to restore historic buildings and bring new homes, creative workspaces and cultural activity back into this part of the city centre.
pullQuotes: Wakefield has some remarkable historic buildings and they deserve to be restored with care
content.text:
The Grade II listed building, to be known as 71 Northgate, will be converted into a series of flexible studio spaces, for makers, artists and small businesses.
The building sits just 100 metres from Wakefield’s historic former Crown Court, to be known ahead as the Court House, where restoration works are already underway. Together, the two buildings form an important part of the Civic Quarter – an area where historic civic buildings are being restored and brought back into everyday use, with new homes, studios and creative spaces returning life to this part of the city centre.

Harry Braid development surveyor at Rushbond said: “The Court House is set to become Wakefield’s most vibrant new destination. It will be a place where everyone belongs - from designers, local radio hosts, independent businesses - all collaborating in the studios; to families enjoying live theatre, music and markets in the Village Hall, all while sharing incredible food and drink. The opportunity to breathe new life into this historic space, together with 71 Northgate is incredibly exciting.” 

Within the wider Civic Quarter vision, 71 Northgate will act as the ‘little sister’ to the Court House, providing smaller-scale studio and enterprise space that complements the larger cultural and events uses planned nearby.

Meanwhile, restoration of Wakefield’s Grade II listed former Crown Court continues, with specialist teams working carefully to preserve the building’s historic features as part of its transformation.
Behind the scenes, specialist teams have been carefully stripping back later additions to reveal and, where possible, salvage original architectural details that will be retained as the building is restored. This reflects the careful, considerate approach required when working with historic buildings of this significance and, in this case, a once-in-a-hundred-years restoration.

When complete, the Court House will reopen to the public for the first time in more than three decades, creating a place for people to gather, work, spend time and enjoy the building as part of everyday city life. The revitalised building also will be a completely new interpretation of the local ‘village hall’ for the new residents who will move into the area.

Jonathan Maud, founder and chairman of Rushbond, said: “Wakefield has some remarkable historic buildings and they deserve to be restored with care, patience and high standards of design and craftsmanship. Projects like the Court House and 71 Northgate are not everyday developments, they are once-in-a-generation opportunities to find sustainable new uses from buildings that have played an important role in the life of the city and aim to do so in the future.

“Our shared ambition for the Civic Quarter is to create something genuinely best in class in terms of build quality, design and the way these historic spaces are used by everyone in the community. Wakefield deserves that level of attention and ambition, and we hope these projects help lift expectations for what is possible in this part of the city centre.”
Elsewhere in the Civic Quarter, the transformation of the surrounding neighbourhood is already visible.

The first phase of 63 homes at the Wood Street Collection was completed last year, bringing new homes into the city centre through the restoration of historic buildings alongside contemporary new housing. The development includes the restored police station apartments, townhouses at Gills Yard and the transformation of Wood House – once the police superintendent’s residence – into a four-storey townhouse.

Six months on, the former Wood Street Police Station is now almost 80% let with just seven apartments remaining to rent. Homes to buy on Gills Mews have also recently been released, with three story townhouses on Rishworth Street available now.

content.title: Parsons Chartered Accountants
Ilkley studio owner launches world class pilates training
content.text:
Following years of intensive training, monitoring and evaluation whilst running her own studio, Kirstin Ferrie, 46, founder of Pure Pilates, has achieved global recognition from one of the most respected and traditional forms of Pilates, Romana Pilates, the world’s oldest and most authentic practice developed by founder Joseph Pilates.

Romana Pilates was born as Romana Kryzanowska, one of Joseph’s students, dedicated her life to preserving his original work exactly as he taught it, and Kirstin has now been mentored and assessed by Romana’s daughter and granddaughter, to become one of the few teacher trainers endorsed and qualified to deliver the world class training in the UK, the majority of which are based in the South.

Kirstin, who has been practicing Pilates since 1997 and teaching it since 2001 said: “Romana Pilates training is recognised worldwide as the epitome of excellence in the industry, and as we continue to see a boom in the uptake for Pilates with over 12 million people now practising it, I’m passionate about helping to keep the standards high, as we read about more and more horror stories of people sustaining injuries when their teachers have not been professionally trained. We’re working with the human body, which is complex and unique to each person. Without proper training, there’s a real risk of injury. High-quality education isn’t optional, it’s essential, and for too long the only place available for this has been down South. How amazing is it that a Yorkshire town is now leading the biggest wellness trend!”.

For her training, Kirstin undertook a vigorous assessment process and continues to train weekly with Romana’s Granddaughter and other leading teachers in the U.K. and Europe, embodying and continuing to improve and deepen her own physical knowledge, passing this onto her students.
Kirstin said: “At this level the smallest tweaks make the difference, the attention to detail and the understanding of how the equipment works with the human body is intricate. There really is nothing like this level of training and I’m so proud to now be able to provide it through my own Centre of Teaching Excellence. “

She added: ‘There is no central body for the Pilates industry. There are no regulations around teaching it and no Government guidelines in place around best practice and standards. With the surge in popularity people can now buy equipment easily and set up as a teacher - this is SO dangerous”.
Becoming a certified teacher within the Romana’s Pilates system is not a quick or easy process. It requires years of intensive training, mentorship, and practical experience. Kirstin, a mum of 2, is now a Level 4 Romana’s Pilates teacher trainer, one of the highest qualifications in this method. She trained through internationally recognised studios and has taught around the world, including in New York, the Caribbean, and Australia. This level of training places her among a small group of teachers globally who are trusted to pass on the method at the highest  standard.
Romana Pilates is a classical method of Pilates that was originally created by Joseph Pilates nearly 100 years ago. His method focused on building strength, improving posture, increasing flexibility, and helping the body move efficiently, without strain. Unlike many modern Pilates classes, which can vary widely in style and quality, Romana’s Pilates follows a structured, time-tested system, where every exercise, sequence, and teaching approach is rooted in the original method. “This is what makes it so respected and so demanding to learn”, explains Kirstin.

Until now, most Romana’s Pilates training in the UK has been based in London and the South. Kirstin’s new centre in Ilkley aims to change that, giving people in the North access to the same elite training
without needing to relocate. Her goal is not just to train instructors, but to raise standards across the industry and she is passionate about the ripple effect this can have on communities.

“I want to build a community of teachers who are not only highly skilled, but also thoughtful and compassionate,” she says. “When we teach well, we can genuinely change how people move, feel, and live.”
Having already had the privilege of helping others progress through the training programme, including Antoinette Brooks-Daw, previously Principal Ballerina at Northern Ballet, she is now excited to continue nurturing the next generation of teachers into the world of Romana’s Pilates.
A workshop and information day will be announced in due course to invite people interested in exploring the training and
experience the difference of how Romana’s Pilates works.

content.title: M does NOT just stand for menopause!
content.intro: The menopause was designed to isolate and separate.
content.text: To strip away our looks, our confidence, our zest for life, and drive us indoors. My response? “Sod that.” And two events I attended last week showed me lots of other women are saying the same. Mythos This annual film conference brings together voices from the creative industries to help unlock opportunities and drive investment across the country, rather than just in the south. I came away BUZZING, especially after watching my clients - screenwriter Jan Birley and director Kathryn Carmichael - take part in a session alongside industry icon Helen Lederer about comedy, creativity and reinvention in later life. We were blown away by the amount of women who approached us afterwards to share their experiences of menopause and the fact that it either encouraged them or stopped them from trying new things  The whole session reinforced the ethos that if we stick together, we can deliver on the need for more films, narratives and art created by women, for women. As we YBW members know, the days of competition are over - it’s collaboration that wins the day! MANIfest For some of us, the menopause is the time when rather than hiding away, we decide it’s now or never and follow that gentle voice that tells us what we should be pursuing. If you call it manifestation or visualisation and throw a few crystals in, it can be met with cynicism. But MANIfest is a safe space for dreamers – and last weekend there were several hundred of them under one roof, with amazing speakers such as Tamu Thomas and Francesca Amber. The event was expertly organised by Mart Tweedy, who I used to work with in the NHS and is now a best-selling author who regularly tops the podcast charts. And all because he followed his dream. Both events are a prime example of what’s possible if you get clear on your vision, believe it’s possible and take aligned action. I leapt into self-employment – totally scared witless - in my forties. I’m now 50 and working on projects I could never have dreamed of had I not taken that first step. So, M does NOT just stand for menopause. It stands for Mythos. It stands for MANIfest. But most of all it stands for movement. Move fearfully or intentionally. If you move in the right direction. And don’t let anything stop you, especially a certain word beginning with M. Claire Kenny is a ghostwriter, PR, and 50 plus blogger. Her insta is @writeforyou444 Claire Kenny (Right)with her sister Rachel Hill at Mythos

Dean Clough to host production for third series of hit TV show
content.text:
Dean Clough, the 22-acre mixed-use destination in Halifax, has been selected for the second time as the main production base for hit TV show High Hoops.
The award-winning comedy, which stars Peep Show’s Robert Webb and Isy Suttie, previously utilised the Dean Clough mill complex as a base for operations for the second series.

Independent production company, Can Can Productions has secured a temporary lease for 5,000 sq ft of space for storage, costumes and set production with filming due to commence next month.
Thea Burrows, head of production at Can Can Productions, said, “We are thrilled to start filming a third series for High Hoops which has been hugely successful. Dean Clough provides an ideal base for production since our set film locations, such as Calderdale College, are so close by.
“The team at Dean Clough are extremely accommodating and flexible to our ever-changing production requirements, with 24-hour accessibility and a secure compound for our vehicles.”

Halifax is rapidly emerging as a significant centre for international film and television production, drawing major companies such as the BBC, Netflix, and Disney Plus to produce and film various projects. Dean Clough, in particular, has served as a filming location for well-known productions including Happy Valley, Ackley Bridge, and Secret Invasion, and has also featured as a backdrop for numerous presenting programmes.

Dean Clough is well known for its cultural contributions, featuring a distinctive underground theatre and one of the largest private art galleries in the UK. The Viaduct Theatre hosts Northern Broadsides, a celebrated resident company whose diverse touring schedule includes Shakespearean works, adaptations of classic plays, and fresh scripts delivered in a northern style, attracting a devoted audience.

It is also a prominent hub for creative industries, serving as home to Calderdale College’s digital creative skills centre, which offers state-of-the-art facilities for studies in film and TV production, design and editing, esports, and games design. Additionally, Dean Clough houses the UK’s largest collection
of historic cinema projection equipment in its basement.

Jeremy Hall, chairman and managing director of Dean Clough, added, “We are delighted to have Can Can Productions and the High Hoops cast join us again at Dean Clough. We love working with them! It adds additional vibrancy and excitement to the community here requiring a quick-fire plan to deliver their filming location as it progresses!
“Dean Clough offers a  lively and diverse range of amenities that, together with its cultural attractions, creates a truly unique environment. You’ll find excellent cafes, bars, restaurants, and fitness, wellbeing, beauty, therapy, and retail services alongside six public art galleries, a subterranean theatre, art studios, and event venues—all within welcoming public spaces and plenty of onsite parking.”

Dean Clough, recipient of the prestigious ‘Development of the Year’ award at the 2024 Placemaking Awards, stands out
as one of Yorkshire’s largest and most influential centres dedicated to the business of arts and culture. The site actively supports commercial enterprise, educational practices, public engagement, and innovation across a wide array of disciplines.
Within the historic mills, the Arts Charity at Dean Clough (ACDC) plays a pivotal role in fostering inclusive arts, business, and education programmes. ACDC’s commitment to accessibility and community engagement was recognised with its own Placemaking award, underlining its contribution to the local and regional arts landscape.

content.title: New holistic care and support for patients at The Rob Burrow Centre
content.text:
Patients and families are benefiting from new holistic care and support at The Rob Burrow Centre for Motor Neurone Disease in Leeds.
Several new sessions and services are being offered to patients and the people who are important to them.

These include mindfulness and relaxation groups, and meditation sessions, which are all open to people from across the MND community in Leeds, West Yorkshire, North Yorkshire, East Riding and the Humber, including patients, families and carers.
A peer support group for bereaved carers is also available for past carers from Leeds and the West Yorkshire region.

Gary Jevon, centre manager, said: “We always wanted the centre to feel different from a traditional clinic and these holistic care groups are a great part of that.
“The mindfulness and relaxation and meditation sessions offer a gentle space for patients and carers to pause, breathe and reconnect. This supports relaxation and a sense of calm through simple, guided practices, including breath awareness, mindfulness and light movement, if possible. Everything is optional and those who attend are free to participate in whatever way feels right for them.

“The Cornflower Group, run by Sam, our family support worker, and the MND Association, gives bereaved carers a space for them to talk and remember a loved one. This was previously running in a service station café and has now been able to move to the new centre, giving past carers a more peaceful and therapeutic setting.
“We are looking forward to developing more groups for patients and families here in the future.”

Another new group, the PEG Café, has been set up for Leeds patients, giving them the opportunity to join an informative and informal chat about Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy (PEG) tubes, which deliver nutrition and hydration directly to the stomach.

Dr Andrew Gill, a palliative medicine consultant who has worked in palliative care in general practice and hospices and is currently based at Airedale General Hospital, will also now be working with motor neurone disease (MND) patients in Leeds.
Dr Gill will be working with patients in Leeds one day a week, helping them manage symptoms and plan for the future. He will talk with patients, and the people who are important to them, about their priorities and wishes. He will also work with patients who have been admitted into hospital, and with those who need home visits.

“When people think of palliative care, they think it’s mostly for older people who are actively dying of cancer, but it’s for anyone with life-limiting illness,” said Dr Gill.
“Palliative care is important right from diagnosis. When people are supported to make decisions all the way through their treatment, it can make a real difference for them in receiving the care they want towards the end of their life.”

People from marginalised groups often have worse access to palliative care and this is something Dr Gill wants to address. “We have to develop palliative care for the needs of the diverse population we serve,” he said.  “Everyone should be able to make decisions about where they want to be and the treatment they want to receive, through their care and towards the end of life.
“It’s really rewarding when you navigate those conversations well and people get the care they want and are as comfortable as possible.”

Dr Gill added: “It is inspirational working here and being part of this team. It feels like a place that’s been inspired by patients, built by patients, and everyone works
together for the patients and the people that are important to them.”

content.title: The Mid-Year Power Edit
content.intro: There is something powerful about the middle of the year.
content.quote: There is something powerful about the middle of the year.
content.text:
The energy of January has passed, the summer season is in full flow, and many women find themselves asking a deeper question: is the life I am building still aligned with the woman I want to become? For female professionals, leaders and business owners, success can often become a moving target. We achieve one goal and immediately chase the next. We hold teams, families, businesses, friendships, homes and expectations together, often without pausing long enough to ask whether the pace, pressure and version of success we are living still feels right. That is why I believe this time of year is perfect for a Mid-Year Power Edit. Not a dramatic reinvention. Not throwing everything away. But a beautiful, intentional pause to edit what no longer serves you and step into the second half of the year with more clarity, confidence and self-respect. As women, we are often brilliant at showing up for everyone else. But leadership, life and success become far more powerful when we also learn to show up for ourselves. That means looking at our energy, our mindset, our diary, our boundaries, our visibility, our wardrobe, our confidence and the rooms we are choosing to step into. The next era of female leadership is not about doing more. It is about becoming more aligned. It is about leading with presence, making intentional choices, feeling confident in how we speak, dress, connect and carry ourselves, and refusing to shrink in spaces we have worked hard to enter. Here are my five transformational tips for your Mid-Year Power Edit:
  1. Edit your energy. Notice what drains you, what inspires you and where you are over-giving.
  2. Edit your diary. Make space for the opportunities, people and experiences that move you forward.
  3. Edit your self-talk. Speak to yourself like the woman you are becoming, not the version of you who doubts herself.
  4. Edit your visibility. Stop waiting to be chosen. Share your voice, enter the room, take the opportunity and own your story.
  5. Edit your style. Your image is not superficial; it is part of your confidence, identity and personal brand.
Success should not cost us ourselves. The second half of the year is an invitation to reset, rise and realign not as a different woman, but as the most powerful version of who you already are. If this resonates, let it be your reminder to pause, reset and choose what feels more aligned and truer. If you are ready for support, I would be honoured to help through The Lavish Collective. Cecil Beaton: Staging Icons at Harewood House
content.intro: Cecil Beaton: Staging Icons (13 June – 4 October 2026) brings together more than 50 unforgettable photographs from the National Portrait Gallery’s collection, some on display to the public for the first time.
pullQuotes: we offer our visitors the chance to step into his glamorous world and see icons, stars, and royals
content.text: Cecil Beaton: Staging Icons (13 June – 4 October 2026) brings together more than 50 unforgettable photographs from the National Portrait Gallery’s collection, some on display to the public for the first time. This summer, Yorkshire’s most vibrant country house, Harewood House Trust, hosts a major exhibition dedicated to the legendary photographer Cecil Beaton (1904 – 1980). Renowned for his innovative theatrical style, Beaton captured some of the most iconic figures of the 20th Century, from Hollywood legends and stars of the West End to the British Royal Family. Organised by the National Portrait Gallery in partnership with Harewood House Trust, Staging Icons offers a captivating journey through Beaton’s extraordinary career as a photographer to the stars. Featuring era-defining portraits such as those of Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Fred Astaire, Queen Elizabeth II and others, the show explores how Beaton’s spectacular approach to staging and design fashioned the identities of his all-star clientele, whilst also revealing Harewood’s own connections to the photographer’s world. From the opulence of the stage to the solemn grandeur of the monarchy, Staging Icons invites visitors to consider Beaton’s approach to image-making through the art of performance and how it continues to shape identity and the public imagination today. Beaton’s first love was the stage, and it left a profound mark on his groundbreaking photographic style. Using elaborate backdrops, theatrical props, costume, lighting and dramatic composition, he blurred the line between reality and artifice, transforming each of his portraits into a work of visual theatre. His passion for creating opulent sets extended to stage and costume design, bringing his unique aesthetic to numerous operas and ballets, as well as stage and film productions in the post-war period. Beaton’s bold creative vision was also instrumental in his work for the British Royal Family. Appointed royal photographer in 1939, his revolutionary portraits propelled the monarchy into the modern age, creating images that were both strikingly glamorous - demonstrated in Beaton’s portraits of Princess Margaret and Queen Elizabeth, The Queen Mother as well as remarkably intimate. Just like his work in show-business, Beaton’s royal portraiture combined elegance and control with theatre, spectacle and fantasy. Staging Icons also explores Harewood’s connection to Beaton and the world of stage and screen, featuring original portraits, artworks and archival material from the Harewood collection. Throughout his career, Beaton photographed numerous members of the Lascelles family and visited Harewood on several occasions during the 60s and early 70s. Several portraits on display feature George and Patricia, 7th Earl and Countess of Harewood, who shared Beaton’s passion for the performing arts. George Harewood was a prominent figure in the world of music, and was a personal friend of many of Beaton’s sitters, such as the opera singer Maria Callas and composer Benjamin Britten. Harewood’s historic visitor book, featuring Beaton’s signature, as well as a Christmas card with a hand-drawn costume design, appears in the show, documenting the photographer’s personal relationship with the family. Cecil Beaton: Staging Icons is organised by the National Portrait Gallery in partnership with Harewood House Trust, marking their first collaborative project. Featuring several never-before displayed portraits, Staging Icons brings the National Portrait Gallery’s internationally significant Beaton collection to audiences in the North of England. Displayed throughout Harewood’s grand State Floor interiors, this major loan is presented against the backdrop Harewood’s own renowned collection of British portraiture, including recent acquisitions such as Ashley Karrell’s powerful photographic portrait of British actor, David Harewood. This work was commissioned as part of Harewood’s Missing Portrait series that seeks to redress the lack of diversity within its historic portrait collection by commissioning new portraits of men and women of African-Caribbean heritage who have contemporary connections to Harewood. Zoë Hughes, head of public programme at Harewood House Trust, commented: “Beaton’s visits to Harewood in the 60s and 70s is just one example of how the site has long been a source of inspiration for artists. Today, Harewood continuously reimagines what makes a historic country house, and by working with the National Portrait Gallery for the first time to bring together Beaton’s work and the House’s rich history, we offer our visitors the chance to step into his glamorous world and see icons, stars, and royals amongst the beautiful backdrop of the House.” Miranda Stacey, head of national partnerships, National Portrait Gallery said “Beaton’s impact on portraiture, and how we visualise British culture, cannot be underestimated. Whether capturing a monarch or a muse, Beaton shaped the public imagination through his use of fantasy, beauty, and the art of performance. Beaton and  the National Portrait Gallery share a long and distinguished history and his first major retrospective, Beaton Portraits, was presented here in 1968. It marked the first time the Gallery had ever exhibited photographs, and the first-time portraits of living sitters were shown, laying the foundations for our enduring commitment to photography. We are thrilled to collaborate with Harewood House Trust to bring over 50 Beaton photographs from our collection to the North, giving audiences the chance to experience the creativity, elegance, and theatricality that defined Beaton’s work.” Cecil Beaton: Staging Icons opens at Harewood House from 13 June to the 4 October 2026. For more information visit: https://harewood.org/events/cecil-beaton-staging-icons/

content.title: Mixing suits with spirits
content.text:
Growing up, Jamila Juma-Ware wore many hats when it came to deciding what she wanted to do when she left education. “In the morning I would want to be a ballerina, then perhaps a schoolteacher in the afternoon and then a police officer by the evening, but always envisioned being busy,” she told us.

After leaving school though, Jamila headed off to The University of Leeds to study French and music, but following a change of heart, switched and graduated from Leeds Met in politics.
Her first job was in public relations and for a long time worked in a variety of in-house teams as head of marketing and in agencies in PR and events, most recently running her own freelance agency, Creative Marmalade, focussing on promoting large scale events to global audiences, including Dubai, South Africa, Washington DC and London.

“Setting up my own business wasn’t difficult, I think anyone can set up a business, but getting the strategy right and having the courage to take the leap from paid employment, to trusting other sources to pay, and on time is the hardest part, and the biggest risk,” she explained. “I’m a pretty risk averse person, but I was lucky enough to have the support of clients in the early days, requesting my marketing service freelance, which led me on my first steps of entrepreneurship. I also had the heavy support of my fiancé, who encouraged me to see my own strengths and believe in them, which helps when you’re making a decision that is outside of your normal comfort zone.

‘Setting up my hospitality and spirit business came a little easier, as I was already working for myself, and in some sense had the perfect side hustle to help bootstrap the business, especially in the early days,” she added. “I’d been supporting one of my PR clients with event management support, including running a themed pop-up bar (with dry ice and a little magic!). My fiancé Matthew had been a travelling tailor for almost 10 years, and we started out by finding the perfect space to transform into a tailor’s studio by
day and a 1920s cocktail bar by night. Tying everything, we do back to a solid strategy, we looked at elements that would make use truly the most authentic and unique speakeasy – and so began our journey in distilling spirits.”

Jamila’s first business set up 11 years ago, the first bar Tailors Speakeasy has been running since 2018 with the original spirit brand Tailors Gin and the full luxury spirit range launched for retail in 2020. A second venue, a literary themed bar and kitchen called Writers’ Bloc launched in Haworth. “I’ve always dreamed of being my own boss and having the flexibility to spend time with family, as much as to build and mould my own future.”
So, what’s a typical day like for Jamila? “Managing a team of 14 and three interconnected businesses means no two days are the same. Day’s range from overseeing operation of both venues, stock, website and social media management to processing retailer and consumer orders for our spirits.
“We are currently looking at our third venue, there are a couple of wild cards up our sleeve which are pretty exciting, but essentially, we want to build and  expand the business footprint and help develop our team alongside this, building opportunity for  not just us, but our fantastic
team that support the operation.”

content.title: Medieval-inspired York aparthotel opens in York
pullQuotes: Success is not final, failure is not fatal...
content.text:
June saw the launch of a new aparthotel in York, a thoughtful and sustainable 21st century response to the medieval history of Micklegate, combining modern comfort with a strong sense of place and heritage.

The 46-suite hotel in Micklegate, which has been designed by leading York architects brown + company, features self-contained apartment units that are aimed at people having longer stays in York.

Blossom Street-based architects brown + company have worked on major York developments such as Coney Street Riverside and the remodeling of the campus at St Peter’s School.

Roger Walters, founder and chairman of Supercity, commented: “Our design team have worked very closely with the team at brown + company. The original exterior was agreed with the City of York Council after careful deliberation to make the building blend in with the character of York.
“It has been a pleasure to work with brown + company.  They have supported us throughout the construction and planning stages. I highly recommend the practice and will use them on our next project.”

This successful development in York is testimony to brown + company’s established practice of working seamlessly with best-in-class partners to deliver unique solutions for complex projects. brown + company worked collaboratively with Montagu Evans, London-based townscape and heritage consultants.

The aparthotel’s surroundings were a key influence on its medieval-inspired design. Micklegate has long presented a streetscape rich in architectural diversity, with the former Roman road playing a significant role throughout each of York’s historical eras.
The name Micklegate, meaning “Great Street,” is derived from the Old Norse Myglagata, while Micklegate Bar later became an important element of the city’s medieval defenses. During the medieval period, a substantial Benedictine Priory dominated the south-east side of the street, while, over time, the north-west side evolved to accommodate the elegant Georgian townhouses that remain today.

brown + company’s design strategy was to create a contemporary 21st-century building that responds sensitively to the context of this historically significant streetscape. The objective was to deliver a solution that enhances the area without adversely affecting the conservation area or its adjacent listed buildings. Working within stringent planning and heritage requirements made this a particularly rewarding project for the architectural team, whose aim was to manage change while preserving the site’s cultural significance.

The design approach drew inspiration from the medieval jettied timber-framed buildings that once occupied the south-east side of Micklegate. A jettied timber-framed building is a medieval construction form in which upper floors project beyond the floor below, creating additional internal space without encroaching on the streets beneath. The scheme also carefully considered rooftop views from York’s historic city walls, as well as key viewpoints along Micklegate itself.
To successfully deliver this complex project, brown + company worked closely with its respected national partner, Leach Rhodes Walker. Their expertise in resolving challenging technical details contributed to a streamlined project experience and successful delivery for the client.

The completed sustainable building preserves Micklegate’s architectural and historic character while delivering a scheme that creates meaningful urban value through placemaking. The development contributes to the continued regeneration of Micklegate, helping to position the street once again at the forefront of York’s tourism and leisure economy.

The aparthotel was initially due to open in 2023 but was delayed by almost a year after part of York’s original medieval wall was found at the site. The site had to be excavated with archaeologists finding items which dated back to the Roman period.
Meanwhile Roger Walters said 12.5 full-time and four part-time jobs will be created by the new hotel. He added that he felt there were few options for businesspeople to make their temporary base while staying in York for longer periods, despite the city’s high number of short-term let properties.

He also hopes the new aparthotel’s city centre location – walking distance from the railway station – will encourage people to stay in York while working nearby, which will help boost the local economy.
“It’s going to bring in a bit more permanency to the visitors, so people will hang around for a few days rather than come in and out of York,” he said.

The new aparthotel features 46 beautifully designed apartment suites that seamlessly combine luxury, practicality, and comfort. Each suite is thoughtfully curated, showcasing a distinctive art collection and original artifacts uncovered during the building’s development, adding a touch of historical charm to the modern amenities.
Facilities include: Lifts; 24 Hour Front Desk; Free Wifi; and easily accessible rooms.
