storyLibrary.title: New head of land and new homes appointed at Northern Estate Agencies Group
storyLibrary.standfirst: Carrie d’Arcy has been appointed head of land and new homes at Leeds-based Northern Estate Agencies Group (NEAG), after long-serving employee, Dawn Carrol, retired from the business earlier this year.
storyLibrary.text:
Carrie, who has more than 14 years’ property market experience, joins from Linley & Simpson where she was senior land and new homes manager, and held responsibility for overseeing the Land & New Homes division in Yorkshire.

Her new role will see Carrie take responsibility for leading and growing the Land and New Homes division across NEAG, which is owned by LRG, and includes estate agency brands Manning Stainton, Ryder & Dutton and Mortimers.

Carrie’s focus will be on strengthening relationships with house builders, developers, landowners and investors, identifying new land and development opportunities, and delivering bespoke sales and marketing strategies for new developments.

She will also support and lead the 36 experienced branch teams to drive sales and increase market share of new homes across NEAG’s extensive regional patch, spanning Yorkshire, Greater Manchester, Lancashire and Derbyshire.

Speaking about her new role, Carrie said: “I’m excited to have joined such a well-respected business with such a strong reputation across Yorkshire and Lancashire. The land and new homes sector continues to face a range of challenges, but it also presents significant opportunities for those who are able to adapt to changing market conditions and buyer expectations.

“What particularly attracted me to the role is the strength of the group’s market-leading brands and the reach they provide across the north of England. By combining this exceptional sales network with our specialist land and new homes expertise, I am confident we can continue to deliver outstanding results for developers, landowners and homebuyers alike.

“My ambition is to build on NEAG’s already strong reputation within the sector, further strengthening our partnerships with developers and landowners across the region.

Mark Manning, managing director of NEAG, added: “We are delighted to welcome Carrie to the group. She brings a wealth of experience across land acquisition and new homes sales and marketing, together with a strong network of relationships built over many years within the property sector.

“A key part of her role will be working closely with developers from land acquisition through to sales completion, helping to maximise development values and ensuring our clients receive exceptional advice and service throughout the development lifecycle. We look forward to seeing her make her mark across the region.

storyLibrary.title: West Yorkshire law firm achieves prestigious accreditation
storyLibrary.standfirst: Calderdale and Kirklees law firm Wilkinson Woodward has achieved Lexcel accreditation, the Law Society’s recognised quality mark for excellence in legal practice management, client care and compliance.
storyLibrary.text:
Awarded following a rigorous independent assessment, Lexcel accreditation is held by fewer than 20% of law firms in England and Wales regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA).

The accreditation demonstrates that Wilkinson Woodward – a long-established practice celebrating its 140th anniversary this year – meets high standards across all aspects of its operations, including client care, risk management, people management, financial management, information management, and file and case management.

The achievement follows a firm-wide project led by risk and compliance manager Clare Ashby, who joined Wilkinson Woodward in April 2025 with the primary objective of securing Lexcel accreditation. Drawing on more than 12 years’ experience of obtaining and maintaining the accreditation at previous firms, she worked closely with colleagues across the business to prepare for the assessment  process.

Laura Kurowski, managing director said: “Achieving Lexcel accreditation is a significant milestone for Wilkinson Woodward and reflects the hard work, professionalism and commitment of Clare and our entire team. We are proud to have achieved this recognition and believe it will give our clients confidence that they are receiving top quality service from a firm that is committed to best practice.”

She added: “While achieving accreditation is an important achievement, it is not the end of the journey. Lexcel requires ongoing assessment and continuous improvement, and we remain committed to maintaining the high standards our clients expect and deserve.”

Lexcel was introduced by the Law Society in 1998 and is recognised as one of the legal sector’s leading quality standards. Accredited firms are assessed against a range of criteria covering client care, compliance, risk management and operational performance, with annual reviews helping to ensure standards continue to be maintained and improved.

storyLibrary.title: Beyond the deal: why the best exits start years before sale
storyLibrary.standfirst: “All right twinkle toes, what’s your exit strategy?” So said Tom Arnold’s character Albert Gibson to the all-conquering spy Harry Tasker (played by Arnold Schwarzenegger) in the 1994 movie True Lies.
storyLibrary.text:
“All right twinkle toes, what’s your exit strategy?” So said Tom Arnold’s character Albert Gibson to the all-conquering spy Harry Tasker (played by Arnold Schwarzenegger) in the 1994 movie True Lies. It’s a question business owners should be asking themselves too, not just those who have already made the decision to sell up, but all business owners.  For leaving it late to draw up a viable exit plan can narrow down the options available which in turn can lead to a less favourable outcome being achieved.

A big decision For many, selling all or part of a business is one of the biggest decisions they will ever make. Sound planning plays a fundamental role in most business successes—it’s what has got you to where you are today along with years, or even decades, of effort and dedication— but for many, the planning only goes so far. For many, it does not extend to exiting. How many? According to a 2019 study by UBS , around half of business owners surveyed did not have a formal exit strategy in place.

All too often owners being underprepared for a sale can have material consequences. This can lead to selling their businesses either in a manner that does not fully compensate them for their years of effort, or the sale takes place at a later point in time than they expect.

A simple solution: plan early Planning early, however, can be easier said than done. Owners tend to be so focused on the running and growing of their businesses that they can neglect longer-term personal plans. And there is no off-the-shelf plan to draw on when the time comes either. That’s because no two entrepreneurs are alike. Key considerations and plans therefore depend largely on what matters most to each individual. This can be a difficult process, and a good starting point is simply identifying what’s personally important to the owner by answering the following questions:

What would you like to accomplish?

Who matters most to you?

What legacy would you like to leave?

The answers require careful consideration and may change in time but giving them some thought can help to frame decisions in the present, as well as for the future. Popular routes for those looking to wind down after selling a business include retirement, travel and spending more time with family.  Whereas those looking to carry on working may consider starting another business or becoming an employee for another company.

How much is enough?

Answering the above questions (or at the very least considering them), allows business owners to have a clearer idea of what they want to get out of a sale or other form of exit when the time comes. This helps inform the answer to another key question: how much is enough? Most business owners have a minimum price at which they would sell but three other factors are also key:

Liquidity: What are the resources required to fund your desired lifestyle? Do you have other sources of income? Will your spending increase or decrease going forward? Have you got a cash buffer for unforeseen developments?

Longevity: The length of expected life after selling the business –different for a 40-year-old than a 70-year-old.

Legacy – What you would like to leave behind for your loved ones? This can mean quite different things for different people.

Answers can vary depending on the aims identified in the pre-sale phase. Retirement and travel require higher sale proceeds than if going into employment for another company, for example. True, the calculations can be quite technical—essentially determining the net present value of future family spending—but the results can provide a degree of clarity which would otherwise not have been possible. And while the results may show a shortfall between the attainable sale value and the desired amount, they could also do the opposite, allowing owners to realise they are able to sell sooner than they expected.

So, whether you are thinking of selling your business or you plan to keep going for a good while longer, it’s time to ask yourself: “what’s my exit strategy?”

storyLibrary.title: New partner for EY
storyLibrary.standfirst: <?ACE 18?> EY has appointed a new partner in Yorkshire, as the firm continues to invest in its regional business and top talent to meet client demand.
storyLibrary.text:
Cara Clancy has joined the partnership in EY’s audit team after more than 16 years with the firm. Cara joined EY’s Leeds office as a graduate in 2009 and has since worked with a variety of audit entities across a range of sectors. Cara has extensive experience of working with companies in the construction and real estate sectors, and she works with several large listed and private businesses in the region.

Cara moved to Yorkshire for university, where she studied psychology at the University of York. She has continued to live and work in the region ever since, as well as supporting colleagues and businesses across the North of England and in London. Cara has also undertaken secondments both with clients and internally, enabling her to build broader business perspectives and a deeper understanding of the opportunities and challenges facing clients.

Cara said: “I’m very proud to have reached this exciting career milestone, and I am looking forward to supporting the continued growth of our business in Yorkshire. Since joining EY’s Leeds office back in 2009, I’ve had the privilege of working with some incredible colleagues and mentors as well as a range of fantastic businesses. I would like to thank everyone who has supported my career journey so far, and I’m excited to see what we can continue to achieve together in the future.”

Kate Jarman, Leeds Office managing partner, said: “I’m delighted to see that Cara’s achievements and dedication have been rewarded with this deserved promotion. She is a highly-valued member of our EY team here in Yorkshire, and I have no doubt she will continue to be a success with the firm. She deserves huge congratulations on this brilliant milestone win her career, and I have every confidence she will continue to build on her accomplishments going forward.”

storyLibrary.title: Knight Frank instructed to market the iconic Elbow Rooms
storyLibrary.standfirst: The Leeds office of the global property consultancy Knight Frank has been appointed to market the unique Elbow Rooms in the vibrant Calls area of the city.
storyLibrary.text:
The Elbow Rooms, once a much-loved bar and night club in the heart of Leeds, has been transformed into a contemporary and stylish office building.

The refurbishment kept much of the building’s original iconic industrial features and exposed brick walls to transform the venue into a variety of functional spaces to be used  as offices.

Victoria Harris, office agency associate with Knight Frank, explained: “We have been instructed to market 2,105 sq ft of high-quality fitted space, which has just come back on to the market after the building was fully let.

“The quoting rent is £25 per sq ft, which represents great value, given the location of the Elbow Rooms, which is next to a host of restaurants, bars, hotels and apartments, and just a five-minute walk from Leeds Railway Station, as well as Leeds’ traditional business and retail cores.

“Meanwhile the mixture of corporate and industrial in the interior of the 24,000 sq ft building is very striking. There’s nothing else like it  around.

“The specific suite comprises modern furniture, meeting room space and a fully fitted kitchen. The occupier will also benefit from access to communal facilities including breakout suite and an additional Zoom/meeting Room. The suite is ready for immediate occupation from September 2026.”

Other occupiers of the Elbow Rooms include digital consultancy Parallax, signage and printing company IPL and branding agency EDNA.

Victoria concluded: “The building can now house a great business which will be able to enjoy the perks of being in the city centre whilst also experiencing a beautiful historic building that is loved by many. Leeds has a growing innovative and enterprising local economy, and we are confident we will soon find an occupier for the space.”

The landlords of the Elbow Rooms are James Brothers Leeds Ltd and the joint agents are Carter Towler.

storyLibrary.title: How Marc Burton started his next chapter at Kirklees College
storyLibrary.standfirst: <?ACE 18?> Marc Burton is a Kirklees College apprentice who is evidence of the fact that it’s never too late to stop learning.
storyLibrary.text:
Having enrolled as an Engineering apprentice in September 2023, Marc has thrived not only at college but also with his employer, Batorer, a precision engineering company based in Cleckheaton. When asked to offer advice to adults who are thinking of retraining and returning to education, he replied: “I think it’s massively important to never stop learning and get re-educated. Having now been through the process myself, I am now living proof that you can teach an old dog new tricks.”

“If you’re stuck in a rut or you don’t love what you’re doing, there is always an opportunity to retrain into something that you’re more passionate about.”

Marc spoke passionately about his journey to this stage, saying: “There was a huge change in my own personal circumstances that made me want to do this.

“I’d previously been a salesman by trade but wanted to do something different with my life.”

Marc added: “I have learnt so much since I started the course. For example, I hadn’t studied Maths since I was at school. My tutor helped me massively with this.” Kirklees College recently launched a new video titled, ‘Your Next Chapter’, which highlights the meaningful impact of adult education at the college. This includes stories from students and apprentices like Marc, who have retrained as adults after a long time out of education.

storyLibrary.title: Entrepreneur who turned £500 into a £1.1m business
storyLibrary.standfirst: Just six years ago, the Yorkshire entrepreneur was running beauty salons and becoming increasingly frustrated after entering industry awards she felt favoured businesses with the biggest marketing budgets over genuine ta
storyLibrary.text:
Just six years ago, the Yorkshire entrepreneur was running beauty salons and becoming increasingly frustrated after entering industry awards she felt favoured businesses with the biggest marketing budgets over genuine talent.
Rather than accepting the status quo, the 28-year-old decided to create her own awards programme built on transparency, accessibility and independent judging.
Today, the UK Hair & Beauty Awards is expected to turn over £1.1 million this year, employs seven full-time staff and has become one of the UK’s largest celebrations of the professional hair, beauty and aesthetics industry.
Taking place at Manchester’s AO
Arena on Saturday 15 August, the event will bring together more than 3,000 professionals from across the UK for a full-day experience including an industry trade show, national awards ceremony and evening festival. Television personality Jake Quickenden will host, while Professor Green, Dappy, Fuse ODG, Tinchy Stryder and Junior Andre headline the entertainment.
For Sophie, however, the biggest achievement isn’t the celebrity line-up.
It’s proving that a young woman from a small Yorkshire town could build a seven-figure business from scratch after spotting a problem that nobody else wanted to tackle.
“I’d entered awards with my salons and was always left wondering how some businesses kept winning,” Sophie said. “It often felt like the companies spending the most on marketing and advertising were the ones walking away with the trophies.
“Everyone in the industry talks about it privately, but very few people wanted to challenge it publicly. I knew there had to be a fairer way of recognising talented professionals.”
Launching the UK Hair & Beauty Awards with just £500, Sophie set out to create an awards programme that gave everyone—from independent beauty therapists and nail technicians to large salons and aesthetic clinics—the opportunity to be recognised based on talent rather than budget.
In less than six years, that idea has grown into a seven-figure business.
“For a long time it was just me doing absolutely everything,” Sophie said.
“I’ve made a lot of sacrifices to get here. My work has genuinely become my life and I still rarely take a day off because I’m constantly looking at how we can improve and make the experience even better.
“I’ve always reinvested back into the business instead of taking big pay days because I’ve wanted to build something that lasts.
“Seeing salon owners and beauty professionals become emotional because it’s the first time they’ve ever felt recognised makes every late night worthwhile.”
This year’s move to Manchester’s AO Arena marks the biggest milestone in the company’s history after outgrowing previous venues.
“The move to Manchester is incredibly exciting,” Sophie said. “It’s a city that’s known for hosting world-class entertainment and major live events, so bringing the UK’s biggest Hair & Beauty Awards to the AO Arena feels like the perfect next step.
“We’re creating something much bigger than an awards ceremony. It’s a celebration of an industry that supports thousands of businesses across the UK, and we’re proud to give those professionals the recognition they deserve.”
Alongside the awards, Sophie is developing a national qualification verification platform that will allow consumers to check whether hair and beauty professionals have the correct training and credentials before booking treatments.
“We want to help raise standards across the industry while continuing to champion the incredible professionals who work so hard every single day,” she said.
From a £500 investment to a business turning over £1.1 million, Sophie hopes her story encourages more young entrepreneurs to back themselves.
“You don’t have to come from money or have huge investment behind you to build something successful,” she said.
“You need resilience, belief, a willingness to keep learning and the
determination to keep going when people tell you it won’t work.”

Sophie Lux is the founder of the UK Hair and Beauty Awards

storyLibrary.title: Schofield Sweeney welcomes private wealth director
storyLibrary.standfirst: Leading commercial law firm Schofield Sweeney has strengthened its private wealth offering with the arrival of director Amanda Simmonds, who joins the firm’s 20-strong specialist team.
storyLibrary.text:
Amanda brings 38 years’ experience as a private client solicitor to the team, advising on all aspects of private client work including wills, trusts and related documents, estate administration, lasting powers of attorney (LPAs) and mental capacity issues, as well as providing advice on inheritance, capital gains and income tax planning.

She has particular expertise in advising family businesses on succession planning and is well versed in complex trust structures, trustee duties, offshore trusts and cross border matters.

Amanda is a member of Society of Trust and Estate Practitioners (STEP) and led the team who drafted the STEP Standard Provisions 3rd edition. She has also been awarded a STEP Founder’s Award, recognising her as an extraordinary volunteer who has gone above and beyond in her dedication to the Society, significantly contributing to its success.

A manda said: “I’m excited to join a team recognised for its collaborative approach, extensive knowledge and personal service. Schofield Sweeney is known for putting clients at the centre of everything they do, and I look forward to working with new clients and building on existing relationships.”

John Feaster, partner, Private Wealth and Succession at Schofield Sweeney said: “I’m delighted to welcome Amanda to our team. She has a stellar reputation in the industry and brings a wealth of experience to our department which now includes nine full STEP members and two chartered tax advisers. I’m excited to work with Amanda to develop opportunities with existing and new clients in the ever-changing world of capital taxes.”

storyLibrary.title: Who’s driving your life?
storyLibrary.standfirst: By Coaching and personal development coach Ros Jones Have you ever reached the end of a day and wondered where it went?
storyLibrary.text:
By Coaching and  personal development coach Ros Jones

Have you ever reached the end of a day and wondered where it went?
You were busy. Productive, perhaps. You answered emails, attended meetings, solved problems, dealt with interruptions and crossed plenty off your to-do list.
“Phew! I got a lot done today”, you might say out loud. And perhaps you did. But did you actually choose how you spent your day? Or did your day simply happen to you?
One of the greatest lessons I’ve learned through coaching leaders over the past thirty years is that many of us slowly hand over control of our lives without ever noticing we’ve done it. It happens insidiously.
Our diary tells us where to be, our inbox tells us what matters, our phone tells us what deserves our attention. Other people’s expectations become our priorities.
Before long, we’re no longer leading our lives. We’re responding to them. Reacting. Psychologists call this a loss of agency.
Agency is our ability to influence our own thoughts, choices and actions. It’s recognising that while we can’t control everything that happens around us, we always retain some control over how we respond.
It sounds obvious. Yet it is astonishing how often we forget.
When we’re stressed, tired or overwhelmed, our brains naturally default to familiar patterns. We become reactive rather than intentional. We operate on habit instead of awareness. Days become weeks, weeks become years, and life begins to feel as though it’s happening at us rather than through us.
Fortunately, agency doesn’t require dramatic life changes. But we do need to wake up!
It all begins with a simple pause.
A single conscious breath before replying to an email. Taking a moment to ask, “Is this really the most important thing right now?” Having the courage to notice that we’re saying yes when we actually want to say no.
These small moments of awareness, repeated, gradually become a different way of living.
As Viktor Frankl famously wrote, “Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response.”
Perhaps that’s the real measure of leadership. Not how much we achieve, not how busy we appear, but how often we remember that the next choice is still ours.
Because the person most responsible for leading your life has always been there, just waiting for you to take the wheel again.
Ros Jones, Business Coach
rosjones@businesswellbeing.club

storyLibrary.title: St Peter’s celebrates 50 years of co-education
storyLibrary.standfirst: 1976: It was a long, and intensely hot summer, inflation was spiralling at 24 per cent, punk music was breaking through - and St Peter’s School in York opened its doors to girls for the first time.
storyLibrary.text:
This milestone marked the beginning of co-education at St Peter’s, which became fully co-educational by 1987, had its first female head prefect in 1989 and is now equally divided between boys and girls.

50 years on, there are now equal opportunities for boys and girls in academics, sport, music and other co-curricular for boys and girls, with the school’s focus firmly the school’s focus on diversity, equity and inclusion.

Jeremy Walker, headteacher commented: “We should be very proud – and thankful – to these five pioneering girls. It must have been very daunting starting that September term 50 years ago, when they didn’t have any idea what to expect. We owe them a major debt.

“I was delighted to be able to co-host an on-line question and answer session with all five girls in 2021 and hear what they felt about being the first girls at St Peter’s, what their experiences had been  at school and how their time here had influenced their future life choices. Their positive answers confirmed that the school’s decision to go co-ed in 1976 was the correct one.

He added: “It is quite astonishing to look back and consider that these five girls were the ones who opened the doors for all those generations of girls and women who followed. There is now a great sense of legacy and history of girls being at St Peter’s.”

Louise Adams, now Louise Morales, an artist and interior designer living in Paris, recalls: “The experience of being one of the first girls at St Peter’s was exciting, daunting and a real privilege. We were special. We were stars. I remember feeling a lot of tension and embarrassment from being in the limelight, but at the same time pleasure.

“There were lots of parties and socialising and we all made friends with the boys. Indeed, Sue and Louise actually married their boyfriends from school. Would I do it all again in hindsight?  Yes.”

She added: “St Peter’s has a sense of history that is so wonderful and we were so privileged to be able to study there. The school gives you the foundation for a fulfilling life.”

The co-host of the old girls on-line Q&A session was Victoria Inness, the first Head Girl at St Peter’s from 1989-1990 and the first female President of the Old Peterite Club. She arrived at St Peter’s in the Sixth Form from York College for Girls.

Victoria, now a corporate lawyer with Knights in York, remembers being called into head teacher Robin Pittman’s study in the summer of 1989 and wondering what she had done wrong.

“I needn’t have worried. To my astonishment and joy, I was told I was going to be the first head girl in the history of the school.

I was incredibly proud and, being honest, I still am today.”

“Looking back at the original decision to admit girls to the Sixth Form 12 years before I arrived at St Peter’s, it was incredibly brave.  Change on this scale, in an institution this old, is never simple.

“And those first five girls required resilience— simply to show up. To sit in rooms where you felt your presence was a novelty. To walk into chapel, through the monkey cage, into lunch and feel conspicuous. To prove, day after day, not that you were special, but that you were simply normal. Simply a pupil, like everyone else. Some might define it as endurance.”

“I imagine it required humility too — a willingness to accept that things were not perfect. To earn trust slowly. To let friendship grow in its own time. The first girls may have arrived with fanfare, they describe feeling like superstars. But they also arrived with quiet determination, and they changed our school for ever.”

By 1986-87, the school had seen enough to know that this was the right path. Girls were welcomed throughout, in every year group. Co-education was no longer a concession.

“When I look back, what I understood very quickly was that I was not representing just myself. I was representing every girl who had arrived before me, and every girl who would come after. That is a weight, but it gives you something to stand for that is bigger than yourself. Ultimately though, despite the apparent significance for others, I was focussed on being not the first Head Girl but simply the best Head of School that I could be.”

She concluded: “What our school gave me and what I hope it gives everyone who passes through it is far more than exam grades. It gave me opportunities that I wouldn’t otherwise have had and a framework for how to be in the world. We, girls and boys, left school ready to take on anything and there is no doubt that as young women we were prepared for a male-dominated work world.”

Yorkshire BusinessWoman 1976: It was a long, and intensely hot summer, inflation was spiralling at 24 per cent, punk music was breaking through - and St Peter’s School in York opened its doors to girls for the first time.

This milestone marked the beginning of co-education at St Peter’s, which became fully co-educational by 1987, had its first female head prefect in 1989 and is now equally divided between boys and girls.

50 years on, there are now equal opportunities for boys and girls in academics, sport, music and other co-curricular for boys and girls, with the school’s focus firmly the school’s focus on diversity, equity and inclusion.

Jeremy Walker, headteacher commented: “We should be very proud – and thankful – to these five pioneering girls. It must have been very daunting starting that September term 50 years ago, when they didn’t have any idea what to expect. We owe them a major debt.

“I was delighted to be able to co-host an on-line question and answer session with all five girls in 2021 and hear what they felt about being the first girls at St Peter’s, what their experiences had been  at school and how their time here had influenced their future life choices. Their positive answers confirmed that the school’s decision to go co-ed in 1976 was the correct one.

He added: “It is quite astonishing to look back and consider that these five girls were the ones who opened the doors for all those generations of girls and women who followed. There is now a great sense of legacy and history of girls being at St Peter’s.”

Louise Adams, now Louise Morales, an artist and interior designer living in Paris, recalls: “The experience of being one of the first girls at St Peter’s was exciting, daunting and a real privilege. We were special. We were stars. I remember feeling a lot of tension and embarrassment from being in the limelight, but at the same time pleasure.

“There were lots of parties and socialising and we all made friends with the boys. Indeed, Sue and Louise actually married their boyfriends from school. Would I do it all again in hindsight?  Yes.”

She added: “St Peter’s has a sense of history that is so wonderful and we were so privileged to be able to study there. The school gives you the foundation for a fulfilling life.”

The co-host of the old girls on-line Q&A session was Victoria Inness, the first Head Girl at St Peter’s from 1989-1990 and the first female President of the Old Peterite Club. She arrived at St Peter’s in the Sixth Form from York College for Girls.

Victoria, now a corporate lawyer with Knights in York, remembers being called into head teacher Robin Pittman’s study in the summer of 1989 and wondering what she had done wrong.

“I needn’t have worried. To my astonishment and joy, I was told I was going to be the first head girl in the history of the school.

I was incredibly proud and, being honest, I still am today.”

“Looking back at the original decision to admit girls to the Sixth Form 12 years before I arrived at St Peter’s, it was incredibly brave.  Change on this scale, in an institution this old, is never simple.

Some might define it as endurance.”

“I imagine it required humility too — a willingness to accept that things were not perfect. To earn trust slowly. To let friendship grow in its own time. The first girls may have arrived with fanfare, they describe feeling like superstars. But they also arrived with quiet determination, and they changed our school for ever.”

By 1986-87, the school had seen enough to know that this was the right path. Girls were welcomed throughout, in every year group. Co-education was no longer a concession.

“When I look back, what I understood very quickly was that I was not representing just myself. I was representing every girl who had arrived before me, and every girl who would come after. That is a weight, but it gives you something to stand for that is bigger than yourself. Ultimately though, despite the apparent significance for others, I was focussed on being not the first Head Girl but simply the best Head of School that I could be.”

She concluded: “What our school gave me and what I hope it gives everyone who passes through it is far more than exam grades. It gave me opportunities that I wouldn’t otherwise have had and a framework for how to be in the world. We, girls and boys, left school ready to take on anything and there is no doubt that as young women we were prepared for a male-dominated work world.”

This framework is reflected and underlined in St Peter’s School Charter, which features four guiding principles: Challenge, community, equity and kindness, with seven key values: Friendship, trust, wisdom, compassion, endurance, humility and hope. There’s no doubt that the arrival of girls at St Peter’s, half a century ago, paved the way for this seminal Charter – and for the success of the school today.

Famous and successful female Old Peterites include sports broadcaster and television personality Kat Downes; Emma Hustler, co-owner of the restaurant chain Tasca Franga; Jenni Ashwood of Filey Bay Whisky and Yorkshire Wolds Beer; and actress Fleur Keith.

This edition, we caught up with Gemma Wright, managing director sales & distribution at Reward Funding, a UK alternative finance provider established in 2010 and headquartered in Leeds. Reward offers asset-secured lending solutions to SMEs across the UK.
Gemma joined Reward as commercial director in 2017 with the responsibility of building and running the operations team across the Leeds and Manchester offices and has played a key role in overseeing the continued growth of the business.
With over 20 years’ experience in financial services with RBS, Gemma’s background was originally in operations before a passion for driving innovation and change led her to move into more strategic roles. Gemma shares her journey so far with us:
“Even before I was born, my dad had grand plans for me to play cricket for Yorkshire - making sure my poor mum headed back to Yorkshire to give birth despite living in Humberside as it was at the time so I could have my ‘Yorkshire passport’,” Gemma explained. “Needless to say, that dream didn’t happen.”
Her own dream was to be a meteorologist - or more accurately, a weather presenter on TV. “I genuinely can't remember when or why it fell away but I think it was around the time I realised I loved languages more than science!
“Because of my passion for foreign languages, I decided to study a combined languages degree at Hull University. Essentially a degree in French, German and Spanish across four years, it involved me studying at university in the UK alongside a period abroad, where I spent most of my time working as an English teaching assistant at a high school in La Rochelle, France.”
Gemma also spent a summer studying at a language school linked to Salamanca University in central Spain, as well as completing an internship in the export department of a trouser manufacturer in Rothenburg, Germany. “I loved my degree,” she explained, “because it fulfilled my two passions, speaking languages and travelling. Hull was also a fantastic university city, where I had lots of fun and made friends for life.”
Growing up, Gemma had the usual part-time waitressing jobs and spent her summers au-pairing in Europe. Her first job post university was working for HSBC in their personal banking call centre. “I went there with a purpose,” she said, “to save enough money to go travelling. So, after nine months, I handed in my notice and went straight to Trailfinders to buy a round-the-world plane ticket!”
Returning home after travelling the world for 12 months, Gemma joined a factoring company in Leeds, Euro Sales Finance. “Perhaps my time at HSBC gave me a thirst for finance,” she explained, “but I think it was more that Euro Sales had offices in France and Germany, so I saw it as an avenue to return to working abroad. What ultimately happened, though, was I got the bug for working in finance, or more specifically for working with businesses and SMEs. I quickly realised that what I enjoyed most wasn’t necessarily finance itself, but getting under the skin of businesses, meeting the owners and hearing their stories. I walked their factory floors to see how everything worked, understood their ambitions and helped them achieve their goals. Twenty-six years later, that’s still the part of my job I enjoy the  most.”
It’s coming up to nine years since Gemma joined Reward following 18 years working at Royal Bank of Scotland. “I was becoming increasingly frustrated with the automation in the banking sector,” she explained, “and lack of appetite to lend to businesses that their algorithms don’t like. I had a huge amount of lending experience at that point but felt I wasn’t empowered to use it, so I wanted to join a company where I could leverage from my experience and go back to basics of supporting business owners. Reward fitted the brief perfectly.”
“And I love it. During my time in finance, I’ve worked in risk, audit, projects and strategy, but I am always pulled back to working with the front-line teams that build and hold those customer relationships. This is what gives me a real buzz,” she continued. “My current role, leading the national sales team, is perfect as it still allows me to interact with the businesses that we support and I also get to grow and develop a team of great people, all of whom are at various stages of their career, to be the best they can. The highlight is seeing the potential in people, coaching them, pushing them to take risks and watching them thrive and achieve things beyond even their own expectations. My proudest moments have been in seeing what my teams have achieved, even more than what I have actually achieved myself.
“One thing I love about working at Reward is that there is no such thing as a typical day or even week! Just in one week for example, I’ve delivered external training with a professional broadcaster, toured a prospective client’s operation, debated strategic initiatives in our board meeting, sat on credit committees and deal clinics, hosted an introducer event on our sun-drenched terrace and even found time to celebrate a colleagues milestone birthday with lunch with the team. No two days are ever the same!”
Reward is at an exciting stage in its journey, Gemma explains: “We’ve invested heavily in our funding structure, systems and people over the last few years and I’m excited to help shape the next chapter. Personally, I still get a huge buzz from seeing talented people develop and helping ambitious businesses achieve their goals. There is plenty more to come from Reward.”
So what advice would Gemma offer to her younger self? “I would say don’t worry about having all the answers. Some of the best opportunities in my life have come from taking a chance, trusting my instincts and figuring things out along the way. I think, looking back, I would have been braver earlier. For years I thought confidence had to come through experience, but I have learned it’s often the other way around,” she concluded.

storyLibrary.title: Clobber Swap launches dedicated website
storyLibrary.standfirst: <?ACE 18?> The Yorkshire founder who built a national swap, buy and sell community from a village Facebook group is launching a dedicated website as major platforms move away from swapping.
storyLibrary.text:
Wakefield West Yorkshire Clobber Swap, the preloved fashion community founded by entrepreneur Camille Johnson, will launch its own dedicated swap, buy and sell website on Saturday 29 August, taking the next step beyond the Facebook group where it began with just 32 local women in January 2020.

The launch comes at a telling moment for the preloved fashion market. Vinted has moved away from swapping to focus on selling, and Nuw, the UK’s best-known dedicated swap app, ceased operations in 2025. Clobber Swap is betting that what the tech-first platforms lacked, it has in abundance: a genuine community.

“Clobber Swap has always been more than a place to buy and sell,” expressed Yorkshire Businesswoman member Camille. “It’s a female fellowship of fashion; women of all shapes, ages and sizes supporting each other, swapping clothes and confidence in equal measure. The new website gives our members what Facebook never could: their own wardrobe boutique, proper search, and listings that don’t disappear down a feed.”

The new platform allows members to create their own online wardrobe, list items in minutes, and swap, buy or sell with other members across the UK – all without commission on sales.

Importantly, the website is being introduced alongside the existing Facebook community, not as a replacement for it. Members can continue enjoying the friendships, conversations, swaps, buying and selling that have defined Clobber Swap from the beginning, while using the website to give their items greater visibility and reach.

Each member will have their own dedicated wardrobe boutique and unique URL, allowing them to share their collections across social media channels, attract more views, and help keep quality fashion circulating for longer.

Sustainability remains at the heart of the business. The fashion industry is responsible for an estimated 10% of global carbon emissions, and Clobber Swap’s model helps extend the life of clothing by keeping garments in circulation rather than sending them to landfill.

“Every swap is a small rebellion against fast fashion,” Camille added. “You refresh your wardrobe, save money during a cost-of-living crisis, and nothing goes to waste. That’s guilt-free shopping.”

Camille, who also co-owns co-working space The Hive Wakefield and marketing agency PAB Studios, founded Clobber Swap during the Covid pandemic after refreshing her own wardrobe whilst swapping with local friends and family. The community grew entirely through word of mouth and has since attracted thousands of members, earned more than 100 five-star reviews, and hosts regular in-person swap events and fashion shows across Yorkshire.

The website launches to the public on Saturday 29 August at clobberswap.co.uk, with existing members receiving early access from mid-August.

Founding Members who join before launch will secure a special membership rate of £3.99 per month. Following launch, membership will be £4.99 per month. Anyone joining before 29 August will lock in the lower Founding Member rate and receive all the benefits of the platform from day one.

Fashion lovers who want to secure the discounted Founding Member rate can sign up now on the website.

“Clobber Swap has always been more than a place to buy and sell,” expressed Yorkshire Businesswoman member Camille. “It’s a female fellowship of fashion; women of all shapes, ages and sizes supporting each other, swapping clothes and confidence in equal measure. The new website gives our members what Facebook never could: their own wardrobe boutique, proper search, and listings that don’t disappear down a feed.”

The new platform allows members to create their own online wardrobe, list items in minutes, and swap, buy or sell with other members across the UK – all without commission on sales.

Importantly, the website is being introduced alongside the existing Facebook community, not as a replacement for it. Members can continue enjoying the friendships, conversations, swaps, buying and selling that have defined Clobber Swap from the beginning, while using the website to give their items greater visibility and reach.

Each member will have their own dedicated wardrobe boutique and unique URL, allowing them to share their collections across social media channels, attract more views, and help keep quality fashion circulating for longer.

Sustainability remains at the heart of the business. The fashion industry is responsible for an estimated 10% of global carbon emissions, and Clobber Swap’s model helps extend the life of clothing by keeping garments in circulation rather than sending them to landfill.

“Every swap is a small rebellion against fast fashion,” Camille added. “You refresh your wardrobe, save money during a cost-of-living crisis, and nothing goes to waste. That’s guilt-free shopping.”

Camille, who also co-owns co-working space The Hive Wakefield and marketing agency PAB Studios, founded Clobber Swap during the Covid pandemic after refreshing her own wardrobe whilst swapping with local friends and family. The community grew entirely through word of mouth and has since attracted thousands of members, earned more than 100 five-star reviews, and hosts regular in-person swap events and fashion shows across Yorkshire.

The website launches to the public on Saturday 29 August at clobberswap.co.uk, with existing members receiving early access from mid-August.

Founding Members who join before launch will secure a special membership rate of £3.99 per month. Following launch, membership will be £4.99 per month. Anyone joining before 29 August will lock in the lower Founding Member rate and receive all the benefits of the platform from day one.

Fashion lovers who want to secure the discounted Founding Member rate can sign up now on the website.

storyLibrary.title: Yorkshire equestrian firm renews official partnership with British Showjumping
storyLibrary.standfirst: <?ACE 18?> Flourishing equestrian bedding manufacturer UNIBED, based at South Milford near Selby, have announced their official partnership with British Showjumping has been renewed for a further three years.
storyLibrary.text:
This comes as the team heads back to the prestigious Royal International Horse Show, held at the famous Hickstead Showground, to celebrate the third year of the UNIBED Winter Grades B&C Championship Final.

UNIBED are a family-run business, centred in their agricultural roots, offering a range of equestrian bedding options all derived from the straw they source from Yorkshire farmers.

The team handle every aspect of production, through to final delivery, ensuring both professional riders and your everyday horse owner, can access good quality, affordable and (now more important than ever) more sustainable bedding for their horses.

The announcement of a renewed partnership follows a successful first three years as an Official Partner to British Showjumping and the Official Bedding Supplier to the National Training Centre.

A spokesman for British Showjumping explained: “We are proud to align with UNIBED, a company renowned for its dedication to optimizing the health and well-being of horses. UNIBED offers innovative bedding solutions that provide superior comfort, absorbency, and durability, while minimizing environmental impact.

“This partnership not only allows us to showcase UNIBED’s high performance equine bedding to a wider audience but also highlights our shared commitment to sustainability.”

Jessica Vickers, commercial and operations director of UNIBED, commented: “We are extremely proud to be continuing our partnership with British Showjumping, a partnership we hold with great regard. British Showjumping is built on a fantastic community of members, who are extremely dedicated to the welfare of their horses.

“This partnership allows to us to showcase what we can offer the equestrian community and spread our message that they do not need to compromise on their horse’s health nor the efficiency of their bedding when choosing a cost-effective option.

“Having UNIBED in the stables at the National Training Centre is a great way for members and those carrying out training – whether that be Team GB or third party training providers – to really give the product a try without any financial commitment and see whether this is something they may want to start utilising when they head back to their own yards.”

storyLibrary.title: Why mediation is becoming the preferred way to resolve workplace disputes
storyLibrary.standfirst: Disagreements in the workplace are an unfortunate reality for businesses of every size.
storyLibrary.text:
Disagreements in the workplace are an unfortunate reality for businesses of every size. Whether they arise from grievances, disciplinary issues, discrimination claims or the breakdown of working relationships, unresolved disputes can quickly affect morale, productivity and the wellbeing of everyone involved.

For both employers and employees, the instinct is often to assume that formal legal action is the only option. However, while employment tribunals have an important role to play, they are not always the most effective or practical route to resolving conflict.

Increasingly, mediation is providing a constructive alternative that allows disputes to be settled more quickly, with less cost and minimal disruption.

A different approach to conflict Unlike tribunal proceedings, mediation is designed to encourage collaboration rather than confrontation. It is a confidential, voluntary process where an independent mediator helps both parties explore the issues, identify common ground and work towards a mutually acceptable solution.

The mediator does not decide who is right or wrong or impose an outcome. Instead, they facilitate productive conversations that might otherwise never happen, giving those involved the opportunity to resolve matters on their own terms.

This approach is particularly valuable in employment disputes, where preserving professional relationships can be just as important as reaching a legal settlement.

The benefits for employers and employees One of the greatest strengths of mediation is its efficiency. Employment disputes that could otherwise take many months to reach a tribunal hearing can often be resolved in a matter of weeks, allowing individuals and organisations to focus on moving forward.

It is also considerably more flexible than litigation. Rather than placing decisions in the hands of a judge, mediation gives the parties greater influence over the outcome, enabling solutions that reflect the practical realities of the workplace as well as the legal issues.

Just as importantly, mediation can reduce the emotional impact of a dispute. Workplace conflict often extends beyond the office, creating stress and uncertainty for those involved. By providing a respectful and structured environment for discussion, mediation can help ease tensions and encourage more positive outcomes.

Supporting businesses through difficult conversations As more organisations recognise the value of early dispute resolution, mediation has become an increasingly important part of the legal services offered by Chadwick Lawrence.

Our accredited mediators combine extensive employment law expertise with practical commercial understanding, helping businesses and individuals navigate challenging situations with confidence. Acting independently and impartially, they ensure that everyone has the opportunity to be heard while keeping discussions focused on finding a workable resolution.

Confidentiality is another key advantage. Unlike tribunal proceedings, which are generally heard in public, mediation allows sensitive issues to remain private. For employers seeking to protect their reputation and employees who value discretion, this can make mediation an especially attractive option.

Looking beyond the dispute Successful mediation is about far more than reaching an agreement. It enables businesses to minimise disruption, protect working relationships where possible and avoid the financial and emotional costs associated with lengthy legal proceedings.

For employees, it can provide certainty, closure and the opportunity to move on with confidence. For employers, it offers a practical way to resolve conflict while maintaining focus on the continued success of the organisation.

While not every dispute can be settled through mediation, many can. Exploring this option at an early stage may save considerable time, expense and stress, making it an increasingly valuable tool for modern workplaces.

Find out more about Chadwick Lawrence’s mediation services: https://issuu.com/chadwicklawrence/docs/chadwick_lawrence_services_brochure?fr=sZTQxYjg1MzI2Mzc.

storyLibrary.title: The room was the highlight of our stay
storyLibrary.standfirst: At the beginning of July, we were lucky enough to be invited to Swinton Park to enjoy an overnight stay, including dinner, bed and breakfast, and access to their award-winning spa.
storyLibrary.text:
At the beginning of July, we were lucky enough to be invited to Swinton Park to enjoy an overnight stay, including dinner, bed and breakfast, and access to their award-winning spa.
For our journey to North Yorkshire, we travelled in the Lexus LBX, which provided the perfect blend of comfort and refinement for the drive. As you arrive at Swinton Park, you’re welcomed through impressive gates with stunning views up towards the estate. Keep an eye out along the approach, as you may spot the deer’s roaming freely across the grounds.
From the moment we arrived, the service was exceptional. We were greeted warmly by the doormen, who helped with our luggage and immediately made us feel welcome. While our bags were taken to our room, we headed inside, where the reception team welcomed us with a glass of fizz to enjoy in the Morning Room.
Before settling in, we took some time to explore the ground floor of the hotel. Each room felt more impressive than the last, but our personal favourite was the beautiful Billiard Room. There’s also a stylish bar area where guests can enjoy an extensive selection of wines, cocktails and other drinks. On a sunny day, we highly recommend taking a seat on the lawn, where you can soak up the picturesque views across the estate.
We were also shown the private dining room, which can accommodate up to 20 guests. It’s a stunning space that would be perfect for an intimate celebration or special occasion, offering an instant ‘wow’ factor the moment you step through the door.
An Afternoon at the Spa
Our next stop was the Country Club, home to Swinton’s award-winning spa. Within moments of arriving, it was easy to understand why it has earned such an excellent reputation.
We spent the afternoon relaxing by the pool and making the most of the facilities. Guests can enjoy a poolside menu featuring light bites, finger sandwiches, sweet treats, and a selection of hot and cold drinks. The spa facilities are extensive, including a thermal suite, hydrotherapy pool, relaxation rooms, saunas and steam rooms, providing the perfect environment to switch off and unwind.
Beyond spa days and treatments, Swinton also offers outdoor wellness experiences in its spa garden, wellness studios and a variety of membership options, making it an attractive spot for both occasional visitors and regular guests.
After a relaxing afternoon, we headed back to the hotel to check into our room.
Staying in the Turret
Our room was undoubtedly one of the highlights of our stay. We were fortunate enough to stay in the Turret, a unique accommodation spread across three floors and filled with thoughtful touches that made the experience feel really special.
The ground floor featured a spacious lounge area, perfect for relaxing after a day exploring the estate. On the second floor was the beautifully presented bedroom, offering stunning views across the grounds. The top floor you will find an impressive bathroom complete with a freestanding bath, walk-in shower, double sinks and dressing area. The room felt warm, inviting and incredibly comfortable.
Dining at Swinton
For dinner, we chose to dine at The Terrace Restaurant. Guests can also choose Samuel’s Restaurant, with each offering a distinctly different dining experience depending on your preference.
The Terrace perfectly reflected the relaxed style found throughout the estate. After enjoying a pre-dinner drink, we settled in for our meal. As we visited on a Sunday evening, we were able to experience Twilight on the Terrace, where live music created a lovely atmosphere for diners both indoors and outside. One of the standout aspects of dining at Swinton is its commitment to estate-grown produce, much of which is sourced from the estate’s own four-acre Walled Garden.
While we were at dinner, the team prepared our room for the evening, leaving a sleep spray on our pillows as part of the turndown service. It’s these thoughtful details that really set Swinton apart and demonstrate the care that the team puts into every guest’s stay.
The Perfect End to Our Stay
The following morning, we returned to the spa for a few more hours of relaxation before check-out. Afterwards, we enjoyed breakfast at Samuel’s Restaurant, where we were fortunate enough to have a table overlooking the estate. Alongside a choice of freshly cooked breakfast options from the menu, there was also a wonderful continental selection of pastries, fresh fruit and other breakfast favourites to enjoy while you wait. It was the perfect setting to enjoy a leisurely breakfast while taking in the beautiful surroundings.
Before leaving, we spent some time exploring the grounds. Swinton Estate has far more to offer than many visitors might initially realise. Alongside the hotel, guests can stay in self-catering cottages or at Swinton Bivouac, while activities range from nature trails and cookery courses to wild swimming and outdoor adventures.
Final Thoughts
It’s probably clear by now that we would highly recommend a visit to Swinton Park. Whether you’re looking for a spa day, an overnight escape, or a family break, there’s something here for everyone.
Looking back on our stay, it’s the little touches that stand out the most – the warm welcome, the stunning setting, the thoughtful service and the chance to completely switch off and relax. We had a lovely time at Swinton Park and wouldn’t hesitate to recommend it, whether you’re visiting for a spa day, a special occasion or a countryside escape. Before we even left the estate, we were already planning our next visit.

storyLibrary.title: "Careers advisers make a difference every single day, helping young people to recognise their
storyLibrary.standfirst: A Yorkshire training organisation founded by professionals who have overcome trauma, adversity and other personal challenges has been chosen by the Department for Education to deliver a major new national training progra
storyLibrary.text:
A Yorkshire training organisation founded by professionals who have overcome trauma, adversity and other personal challenges has been chosen by the Department for Education to deliver a major new national training programme designed to improve careers advice for young people facing some of the biggest barriers to education and employment.

The Department for Education has announced that Yorkshire-based Transform Your Training will lead the design and delivery of England’s new national Continuing Professional Development (CPD) programme for careers advisers, following a competitive procurement process.

Designed by experts who have themselves overcome barriers to progression, the new national programme aims to transform careers advice for young people across England, as the Department for Education steps up its efforts to meet the Government’s Back to Work commitments.

Founded by Tammy Banks and Faye Fox after successful careers in York’s charity sector, Transform Your Training has spent the last decade supporting local authorities, charities, schools and public services across Yorkshire. Today it is a trusted partner to City of York Council, delivering leadership development, safeguarding and domestic abuse programmes. The Department for Education’s appointment builds on those Yorkshire foundations, taking an approach developed through local partnerships, lived experience and real-world practice to careers professionals across England Using its award-winning Training 4 Influence methodology, Transform Your Training – which employs 20 people from its Lowther Street base, as well as working with an extended team of 100 facilitators across the country - will shape a programme that combines trauma-informed, expert facilitation with practical application, collaboration and values-led learning. Importantly, the training will be designed and delivered by facilitators with personal and/ or professional lived experience of the barriers many young people face, adding a deep level of understanding and insight that will unlock the transformative power of training.

The contract to deliver the programme on behalf of the Department for Education builds on the life’s work of Transform Your Training co-founder and CEO, Tammy Banks, who is leading the mission that quality, values-led training can transform lives. Tammy, who lives in the city, channels her own lived experience, passion and over 20 years’ professional experience into championing change and seeking creative ways to interrupt the generational cycle of harm and abuse. She believes the programme represents a vital opportunity to unleash the potential of hundreds of thousands of young people in England, by enabling careers advisers to better support them to recognise opportunities, overcome barriers and make informed choices about their futures.  It is expected that Transform Your Training’s contract win with the DfE will enable the company to create seven new roles.

Tammy said: “Careers advisers make a difference every single day, helping young people to recognise their strengths and open doors to opportunities that can shape the rest of their lives.  That impact can be amplified if – through their own professional development – we are able to support careers advisers to understand and respond to the needs of young people who face barriers – whether they’re young people in the care system or people who have experiences trauma or adversity. “Every young person deserves access to high-quality careers guidance, whatever their background or circumstances.  It’s something I am hugely passionate about because of my own experience of navigating adverse experiences and significant challenge as a young person and having to advocate for myself in order to get the life chances I deserved.  Values-led quality training can drive this change for young people today; it can motivate and inspire careers advisers and connect them to the young people they serve in new ways.”

She added: “Training that values the people in the room, that thanks them for the work they’re doing, that teaches them the skills, models and values to really work with the people accessing their services in an equal and equitable way is vital.  It can transform lives and revolutionise our public services. I believe this CPD programme can support careers advisers to unlock the potential of generations of young people who might otherwise never be able to see past the barriers in front of them. This is a huge opportunity to do things differently and make a massive impact.”

Tammy’s personal history, academic achievements and work experience have driven her to champion the importance of effective solutions within organisations working with people who are marginalised or disadvantaged.  Her own childhood was impacted by harm, abuse and neglect – experiences that now fuel a deep personal desire to ‘change the system’.  It was a teacher at Inspire Education Group  – where Tammy is now a Governor – listening to her as a child seeking education, who first unlocked Tammy’s belief that she could aspire to be and achieve much more.

“Adults in schools and colleges have the power to change the lives of the young people they work with – whether they’re teachers or careers advisors.  That’s why I believe values-led quality training for careers advisers who work with young people day-in and day-out can transform lives and create a ripple effect across society.  I’ve seen it in my own practice – the power of sharing my experiences as part of a structured, tailored programme of training to ensure there is not only intellectual learning, but emotional learning too.  To now have the opportunity to directly impact on the delivery of careers advisers in England through Transform Your Training’s network of facilitators – each of whom will bring personal and/ or professional lived experience - feels like a milestone moment in what is a deeply personal mission for me. Our young people deserve equity of opportunity.”

Transform Your Training’s appointment reflects a shared ambition with DfE to strengthen the consistency and quality of careers guidance across England and ensure more young people receive guidance that helps them to build brighter futures.

The programme will launch  in October.  Careers professionals from schools, colleges, universities and alternative provisions  can access the training for  free, and it will be delivered through national inspiration conferences, six continuing professional development (CPD)  modules, monthly expert panels and a community of practise.

To sign up for more information about the programme, visit www.transformyourtraining.org/national-careers-adviser-cpd-programme. And to find out more about Transform Your Training and its Training 4 Influence methodology, visit https://transformyourtraining.org "Careers advisers make a difference every single day, helping young people to recognise their strengths and open doors to opportunities..."
