The Department for Education’s appointment builds on those Yorkshire foundations, taking an approach developed through local partnerships, lived experience and real-world practice to careers professionals across England Using its award-winning Training 4 Influence methodology, Transform Your Training – which employs 20 people from its Lowther Street base, as well as working with an extended team of 100 facilitators across the country - will shape a programme that combines trauma-informed, expert facilitation with practical application, collaboration and values-led learning. Importantly, the training will be designed and delivered by facilitators with personal and/ or professional lived experience of the barriers many young people face, adding a deep level of understanding and insight that will unlock the transformative power of training.

The contract to deliver the programme on behalf of the Department for Education builds on the life’s work of Transform Your Training co-founder and CEO, Tammy Banks, who is leading the mission that quality, values-led training can transform lives. Tammy, who lives in the city, channels her own lived experience, passion and over 20 years’ professional experience into championing change and seeking creative ways to interrupt the generational cycle of harm and abuse. She believes the programme represents a vital opportunity to unleash the potential of hundreds of thousands of young people in England, by enabling careers advisers to better support them to recognise opportunities, overcome barriers and make informed choices about their futures.  It is expected that Transform Your Training’s contract win with the DfE will enable the company to create seven new roles.

Tammy said: “Careers advisers make a difference every single day, helping young people to recognise their strengths and open doors to opportunities that can shape the rest of their lives.  That impact can be amplified if – through their own professional development – we are able to support careers advisers to understand and respond to the needs of young people who face barriers – whether they’re young people in the care system or people who have experiences trauma or adversity. “Every young person deserves access to high-quality careers guidance, whatever their background or circumstances.  It’s something I am hugely passionate about because of my own experience of navigating adverse experiences and significant challenge as a young person and having to advocate for myself in order to get the life chances I deserved.  Values-led quality training can drive this change for young people today; it can motivate and inspire careers advisers and connect them to the young people they serve in new ways.”

She added: “Training that values the people in the room, that thanks them for the work they’re doing, that teaches them the skills, models and values to really work with the people accessing their services in an equal and equitable way is vital.  It can transform lives and revolutionise our public services. I believe this CPD programme can support careers advisers to unlock the potential of generations of young people who might otherwise never be able to see past the barriers in front of them. This is a huge opportunity to do things differently and make a massive impact.”

Tammy’s personal history, academic achievements and work experience have driven her to champion the importance of effective solutions within organisations working with people who are marginalised or disadvantaged.  Her own childhood was impacted by harm, abuse and neglect – experiences that now fuel a deep personal desire to ‘change the system’.  It was a teacher at Inspire Education Group  – where Tammy is now a Governor – listening to her as a child seeking education, who first unlocked Tammy’s belief that she could aspire to be and achieve much more.

“Adults in schools and colleges have the power to change the lives of the young people they work with – whether they’re teachers or careers advisors.  That’s why I believe values-led quality training for careers advisers who work with young people day-in and day-out can transform lives and create a ripple effect across society.  I’ve seen it in my own practice – the power of sharing my experiences as part of a structured, tailored programme of training to ensure there is not only intellectual learning, but emotional learning too.  To now have the opportunity to directly impact on the delivery of careers advisers in England through Transform Your Training’s network of facilitators – each of whom will bring personal and/ or professional lived experience - feels like a milestone moment in what is a deeply personal mission for me. Our young people deserve equity of opportunity.”

Transform Your Training’s appointment reflects a shared ambition with DfE to strengthen the consistency and quality of careers guidance across England and ensure more young people receive guidance that helps them to build brighter futures.

The programme will launch  in October.  Careers professionals from schools, colleges, universities and alternative provisions  can access the training for  free, and it will be delivered through national inspiration conferences, six continuing professional development (CPD)  modules, monthly expert panels and a community of practise.

To sign up for more information about the programme, visit www.transformyourtraining.org/national-careers-adviser-cpd-programme.  And to  find out more about Transform Your Training and its  Training 4 Influence methodology, visit https://transformyourtraining.org

storyLibrary.title: Yorkshire Traveller inspires the Next Generation
storyLibrary.standfirst: A Yorkshire entrepreneur who has travelled and explored 57 countries across five continents - from riding motorbikes across the Himalayas, exploring the jungles of Borneo and camping beneath the stars in Africa - is now
storyLibrary.text:
A Yorkshire entrepreneur who has travelled and explored 57 countries across five continents - from riding motorbikes across the Himalayas, exploring the jungles of Borneo and camping beneath the stars in Africa - is now using a lifetime of adventure to inspire the next generation of explorers.
Gemma Herron, 53 from Leeds, has launched Colour the World, a collection of screen-free travel adventure books, explorer packs and educational resources for children aged 5-11. Created from more than twenty years of travelling the world, the books are designed to spark curiosity about different countries, cultures and wildlife, helping children discover the joy of exploring long before they ever board a plane.
“Travel has shaped every part of who I am,” says Gemma. “I wanted to create something that would give children that same sense of curiosity and wonder I discovered through travelling.”
Gemma’s love of travel began in Garforth, Leeds, where she grew up, Gemma explains; “I was a quiet, bookish girl who didn’t quite fit in. I had a huge imagination and an even bigger curiosity about the world beyond my own street. I’d read about countries and cultures for hours, but travelling felt impossibly far away. I always knew I wanted to see the world. I just didn’t know how.”
But, Gemma’s first opportunity came in her early twenties when she packed a bag and travelled alone to France to work for Eurocamp. She returned the following season to Majorca as a children’s entertainer, spending her days inventing games and activities for hundreds of children.
Looking back, she now realises two lifelong passions were beginning at exactly the same time. “I fell in love with travel... and I fell in love with seeing the world through children’s eyes.” And, those two passions would eventually become her new business ‘Colour the World’, although it would take another two decades - and 57 countries - for the idea to fully take shape!
For most of her twenties, Gemma continued to work on campsites in France, Switzerland and Mallorca. But, she got the wanderlust bug when she first travelled to India for 6 months in 1999. Gemma explains; “It was my first trip outside of Europe. I’d never even eaten Indian food before I went. Looking back that probably tells you everything about how sheltered my world was at that point. The first two weeks were quite hard - India doesn’t ease you in gently. It just arrives, all at once, at full volume. But soon, something shifted and in those six months, India stopped being overwhelming and started being extraordinary. The kindness of strangers. The colour of everything. The way food I’d never tasted before suddenly became the best thing I’d ever eaten. The way people with so little seemed to carry so much joy. And, for the first time, I wasn’t just visiting somewhere. I was truly seeing it. And once you learn to see the world that way - with genuine wonder - you can never go back.”
However, by her late twenties, Gemma felt it was time to settle down. She built a successful corporate career in learning and development, bought a house, got married and embraced the life she believed she was supposed to want. But the traveller in her never disappeared. Every annual leave allowance became another opportunity to explore somewhere new.
Looking back, Gemma says she was following the path she thought was expected of her. “On paper, everything looked right, but I
slowly realised I’d become tied to a monthly salary and counting down my holiday allowance. I was becoming more risk-averse, and the freedom I craved was limited to a few weeks each year. Deep down, I knew there had to be another way to live.”
At work, Gemma’s team was facing a major restructure, with roles being reshuffled and redundancies on the horizon. Rather than wait to see what would happen, she initially decided to play it safe and applied for another role within the company. Much of the restructuring process unfolded while Gemma was away on another adventure, riding motorbikes across the Himalayas with her husband. When she returned home, she had a ‘now or never’ moment and decided it was time to leave the corporate world behind. To her husband’s surprise, she accepted voluntary redundancy, knowing it was her opportunity to choose a different way of living. She and Mark rented out their Yorkshire home and returned to seasonal work in France and Switzerland, spending each winter exploring a new corner of the world.
Over the next twelve years, they travelled extensively across Asia, Africa and the Americas - travelling the length of Vietnam, exploring Patagonia by campervan, camping across Botswana and South Africa, and returning to India time and again.
But, Gemma says, it wasn’t the landscapes that changed her most… “it was the people. Wherever we went, complete strangers welcomed us into their homes, shared meals with us, helped us when we were lost and showed us incredible kindness. It taught me something I wish every child could grow up knowing - that the world is overwhelmingly full of good people.”
Then life took an unexpected turn. While living and working seasonally in Switzerland, Mark was diagnosed with cancer. “It stops you in your tracks,” says Gemma. “One day you’re planning your next adventure, and the next you’re sitting in a hospital wondering what the future looks like.” Mark underwent treatment and surgery in Switzerland, and thankfully went on to make a full recovery. The experience was a profound reminder of how precious life is and strengthened a belief they had been building throughout their years of travel - that they were choosing the right way to live. Gemma explains; “It reinforced something we’d already started to believe - that life is far too short to keep waiting for the perfect moment. We spend so much of our lives saying ‘one day’. But life doesn’t always give you one day. We realised the memories we’d collected together weren’t the reward for living - they were the point of living.”
Rather than making them step away from their adventurous lifestyle, it reinforced their desire to embrace every opportunity, continue exploring the world, and make the most of their time together. Gemma and Mark continued working seasonally for several more years, until changes brought about by Brexit eventually made that way of life more difficult to continue.
Back in Yorkshire, Gemma found herself thinking about the little girl she had once been - the quiet child in Leeds who dreamed of seeing the world but had no idea where to begin. That became the inspiration behind Colour the World - and, despite its name, it is about far more than colouring… The growing collection of screen-free travel adventure books, explorer packs and educational resources encourages children to discover countries, cultures, wildlife and traditions through puzzles, stories, games, creative challenges and hands-on activities... colouring is simply one part of the adventure.
“I don’t just want to keep children entertained,” says Gemma. “I want them to fall in love with the world.”
Having travelled to 57 countries, worked with children across Europe and helped people with their holiday and travel, Gemma believes curiosity is one of the greatest gifts a child can have.
She said; “I’ve seen incredible beauty and kindness everywhere I’ve travelled. Children are naturally curious about the world, and I want to help nurture that curiosity. Because a child who falls in love with the world grows up wanting to protect it, celebrate it and share it with others.”
Gemma and Mark continue to spend their summers working on campsites in Yorkshire while using the autumn and winter months to explore the world, with Georgia, Istanbul and Azerbaijan next on
their ever-growing list of adventures.

Louise Reed is one of Yorkshire’s most influential community figures. Her journey into charitable work began in 2016, triggered by the widely publicised image of Alan Kurdi, a two yearold Syrian boy who drowned while crossing the Mediterranean Sea with his mother and brother. With daughters of a similar age, the tragedy struck her deeply and she began volunteering to support refugees in crisis, including facilitating dental treatment through partnerships with Town Hall Dental.

While helping abroad, Louise recognised the scale of need at home, worsened when the COVID pandemic struck in 2019. She gathered friends and professional contacts to form a community group, which later became Focus4Hope and achieved full charity status in November 2020. Now approaching its tenth anniversary, it’s become a lifeline for people who are isolated, vulnerable and disadvantaged. This includes homeless people, elderly people, domestic abuse survivors, and refugees.

Homelessness has doubled in the past year and Louise wants Focus4Hope to continue to rise to the occasion, increasing the volume of vital services in a bid to avoid individuals reaching crisis point. The charity is already planning for Christmas, including its hamper project (over 550 were delivered last year), gifts for children and young adults, and grants for heating.

Louise leads the charity tirelessly, doing everything in her power to balance grassroots support with strategies to grow the team, raise awareness and mobilise entire communities. She also coordinates largescale fundraising events, including Focus4Hope’s ten-year anniversary ball. On Saturday 19th September in Brighouse, the ball is hosted by presenter, influencer, reality TV star and Focus4Hope ambassador Matt Jameson. Tickets can be purchased at focus4hope.co.uk More broadly, Louise’s aim is to secure long-term support from businesses and donators to enable Focus4Hope to continue to respond to increasing demand attached to the rising cost of living. A vital part of this is highlighting the role business leaders and social influencers can play in supporting the broader community and the benefits in the form of stronger brand reputation, positive PR, higher customer loyalty, and tax efficiency.

While people need support, Louise are her team are determined to provide it.

storyLibrary.title: Some founders build business, Victoria built a world
storyLibrary.standfirst: Some founders build businesses.
storyLibrary.text:
Some founders build businesses. Victoria built a world — because she knows how powerful a moment can be.
After being told she had cancer, Victoria experienced the fear, the uncertainty, and the daily fight that changes how you see everything. Almost 11 years on — and after beating cancer three times — she chose to flip the card she was dealt and turn something devastating into something meaningful: a life led with purpose, perspective, and an unwavering commitment to making every moment count.
That mindset is the heartbeat of NVRLND.
NVRLND is a luxury entertainment and events agency creating surreal, show-stopping experiences for corporate clients and agencies — where professionalism is non-negotiable and the detail is everything. From high-impact brand activations to immersive entertainment and unforgettable corporate Christmas parties, we transform spaces into worlds and events into stories people still talk about long after the lights go down.
If you’re looking for an events partner who brings creative vision, calm delivery, and a signature sense of wonder — we’d love to build something extraordinary with you.
NVRLND — where reality meets wonderland.
www.nvrlnd.uk Instagram: @nvrlnd.uk

YorkshireBusinessWoman

Victoria Eames is the Founder of NVRLND. Creator of wonderlands.

storyLibrary.title: Welcome to Wakefield: The UK’s Capital of Sculpture
storyLibrary.standfirst: <?ACE 18?> The Wakefield district is a destination that has turned a proud industrial past into a bold new identity, home to a cathedral city, charming market towns, stunning rural scenery and some of the UK’s leading ar
storyLibrary.text:
The Wakefield district is a destination that has turned a proud industrial past into a bold new identity, home to a cathedral city, charming market towns, stunning rural scenery and some of the UK’s leading art and cultural attractions.

As the UK’s capital of Sculpture, it is firmly establishing itself as the cultural gateway to the north and deserves a place on every culture and experience seeker’s bucket list.

At the heart of the district’s cultural offer are award-winning galleries Yorkshire Sculpture Park and The Hepworth Wakefield, showcasing world-class art by international icons. Yet Wakefield’s creative story extends far beyond its flagship attractions.

From the grassroots creativity of the studios and galleries of The Art House and Neon Workshops to the creative powerhouses of Tileyard North, Production Park and WX Wakefield Exchange, culture can be found in unexpected places across the district.

Public art makes a statement, inviting cultural participation beyond the galleries in parks, landscapes, town centres, and urban spaces. Beyond its artistic credentials, visitors can enjoy a rich mix of heritage at attractions like the National Coal Mining Museum for England, Pontefract Castle and National Trust Nostell, independent food and drink, festivals (including the UK’s largest Pumpkin Festival, the north’s largest Tulip Festival and celebrations of the district’s homegrown heroes, Rhubarb and Liquorice),outdoor adventure, and family attractions like Xscape, N ational Trust Nostell and Diggerland.

Perfectly positioned in the heart of Yorkshire, well connected at the crossroads of major motorways and just two hours from London by train, Wakefield is easy to get to and rewarding to explore. Whether visiting for a day, a weekend or longer, there is more to discover than many people realise.

You are invited to discover  Wakefield - the UK Capital of Sculpture.

storyLibrary.title: Meet the entrepreneur redefining healthy living in Ripon
storyLibrary.standfirst: Just months after opening its doors, Sustain has firmly established itself as one of Ripon’s newest independent success stories, bringing together health, wellbeing and community in the heart of the city.
storyLibrary.text:
Founded by Charlotte Baldwin, Sustain has transformed one of Ripon’s most recognisable retail spaces at the historic Halls of Ripon into a vibrant destination offering carefully selected health foods, supplements, sustainable products and a welcoming coffee shop.

Since launching earlier this year, the business has built a loyal customer following.

Charlotte founded Sustain after working in the independent health food sector, inspired by a desire to create a space that offered far more than retail.

“I wanted to create the kind of place I always felt should exist,” she said. “Somewhere that doesn’t just sell products, but actually helps people, whether that’s understanding what to eat, finding support through different stages of life or simply feeling more like themselves again.”

That support is designed to meet people where they are. For some, it might be guidance through menopause, with trusted advice, nutrition and practical resources. For others, it’s as simple as a parent finding genuinely healthy snacks their child will enjoy, without the sugar highs or additives. “I want people to feel energised, joyful and well, whatever stage of life they’re in,” Charlotte added.

That philosophy is reflected throughout the business. Alongside its carefully curated retail offering, Sustain’s coffee shop provides a welcoming place for people to pause, while customers can also explore organic wines using the shop’s Enomatic wine machine, sampling different varieties in a relaxed setting. Charlotte also plans to develop a programme of events, workshops and collaborations with local wellbeing practitioners, creating opportunities for people to learn, connect and prioritise their wellbeing.

One of the building’s most striking features is a medieval well uncovered during renovations, which has become an integral part of Sustain’s identity and future plans.

The business was officially opened by the Mayor of Ripon earlier this year, marking another milestone in the regeneration of the historic Halls site and reinforcing the important role independent businesses continue to play in attracting people back to the high street.

Charlotte believes the business’s success reflects a growing demand for places that prioritise both wellbeing and connection.

“People are looking for somewhere they feel welcome,” she said. “Whether someone comes in for advice, to enjoy a coffee with friends, discover new products or attend one of our events, we want Sustain to be somewhere that helps people feel energised, supported and inspired.”

As Sustain continues to grow, plans are underway to expand its programme of events, workshops and partnerships, further strengthening its role  as a destination for healthy living and community in Ripon.

Charlotte added: “It’s been incredible to see the response from the local community. We’re proud to be part of Ripon’s independent business scene and excited about what’s still to come.”

storyLibrary.title: Stop seeking permission: Your presence is your power
storyLibrary.standfirst: “The moment you stop seeking permission to be yourself is the moment your presence becomes unforgettable.” - Lisa Darwin How often do women wait for permission?
storyLibrary.text:
“The moment you stop seeking permission to be yourself is the moment your presence becomes unforgettable.” - Lisa Darwin
How often do women wait for permission?
Permission to speak, lead, change direction, take up space, wear something bold, launch a business or pursue an ambition that others may not understand.
From an early age, many women learn to seek approval. We question whether we are experienced enough, qualified enough, young enough, polished enough or even whether we are simply “too much.” As a result, we can spend years editing ourselves to fit the expectations of others.
Yet the most memorable women in business are rarely those who disappear comfortably into the background. They are the women who know who they are, understand what they stand for and bring their personality, values and lived experience into the room.
Authenticity is not about sharing everything or demanding attention. It is about alignment. It is the confidence to allow the person you are privately to match the person you present professionally.
When we stop performing a version of success and begin defining it for ourselves, something changes. Our communication becomes clearer. Our decisions become stronger. We attract people and opportunities that genuinely connect with our purpose.
This is also where personal style can become powerful. What we wear should not disguise us or force us into somebody else’s idea of professionalism. It should support our identity and help us walk into a room feeling confident, credible and completely ourselves.
Of course, becoming more visible can feel uncomfortable. The fear of judgement does not disappear overnight. But confidence is not the absence of fear; it is choosing to move forward while fear is still present.
You do not need permission to evolve. You do not need permission to begin again, raise your prices, share your ideas, enter a new room or become more ambitious about your future.
The right people will not require you to make yourself smaller in order to belong.
Yorkshire is filled with extraordinary businesswomen leading companies, creating employment, supporting communities and opening doors for others. Our collective responsibility is to create more rooms where women are encouraged to be seen, heard and celebrated for who they truly are.
Your difference is not a disadvantage. Your story is not something to hide. Your voice does not need to sound like anybody else’s.
Stop waiting to be chosen. Choose yourself and allow the world to remember you.
In September, I am launching The Lavish Collective Pathways: transformational coaching created to help women strengthen their identity, elevate their confidence and achieve greater success in life and business.
Ready to stop seeking permission and become unforgettable? I would be honoured to help you step into your power. E: lisa@lisadarwin.com W: www.lisadarwin.com

with Lisa Darwin, transformational Coach

storyLibrary.title: Wear the Woman You’re Becoming
storyLibrary.standfirst: There is a moment in every entrepreneur’s journey when the world hasn’t quite caught up with the vision in your head.
storyLibrary.text:
There is a moment in every entrepreneur’s journey when the world hasn’t quite caught up with the vision in your head. The business is still growing, the opportunities haven’t all arrived, and some days you’re running purely on determination. Yet every morning, you still get up, get dressed and show up.
I’ve always believed that what we wear is about far more than fashion. It’s about how we choose to present ourselves to the world, but perhaps more importantly, how we remind ourselves who we are. The right outfit won’t build a business or close a deal, but it can help you walk into a room with confidence, even on the days when self doubt is quietly whispering in the background.
As women in business, we often wear many hats. We’re leaders, creatives, problem-solvers cheerleaders for everyone around us, mothers, partners and what feels like at times the woman everyone wants a piece of. (Well that’s certainly how I feel) It’s easy to put ourselves at the bottom of the list, throwing on whatever is closest because there are emails to answer, meetings to attend and deadlines to meet. But taking a moment to dress with intention is not vanity; it’s an investment in how we feel.
Confidence isn’t always something we’re born with. Sometimes it’s something we create. A beautifully tailored jacket, a dress that fits perfectly or a colour that makes you feel your best can become a quiet reminder of the woman you’re working so hard to become. It’s not about expensive labels or following every trend. True style comes from authenticity, quality and wearing clothes that make you feel like yourself.
Over the years, I’ve met countless women through my work, and while every story is different, one thing
remains the same. The most stylish women aren’t necessarily the ones with the biggest wardrobes; they’re the ones who wear their confidence with grace. They understand that getting dressed is not about impressing others it’s about stepping into the best version of themselves.
So the next time you stand in front of your wardrobe before an important  meeting, networking event or simply another busy day, remember that you’re not just choosing what to wear. You’re choosing how you want to feel.
Wear the woman you’re becoming. She deserves to be seen long before the rest of the world catches up.
Rebecca x
Rebecca Rhoades’ craft is not about following trends - it is about designing garments that endure, that embody presence, and that speak without words. Visit her website to find out how Rebecca can help you.

There is a moment in every entrepreneur’s journey when the world hasn’t quite caught up with the vision in your head. The business is still growing, the opportunities haven’t all arrived, and some days you’re running purely on determination. Yet every morning, you still get up, get dressed and show up.

I’ve always believed that what we wear is about far more than fashion. It’s about how we choose to present ourselves to the world, but perhaps more importantly, how we remind ourselves who we are. The right outfit won’t build a business or close a deal, but it can help you walk into a room with confidence, even on the days when self doubt is quietly whispering in the background.

As women in business, we often wear many hats. We’re leaders, creatives, problem-solvers cheerleaders for everyone around us, mothers, partners and what feels like at times the woman everyone wants a piece of. (Well that’s certainly how I feel) It’s easy to put ourselves at the bottom of the list, throwing on whatever is closest because there are emails to answer, meetings to attend and deadlines to meet. But taking a moment to dress with intention is not vanity; it’s an investment in how we feel.

Confidence isn’t always something we’re born with. Sometimes it’s something we create. A beautifully tailored jacket, a dress that fits perfectly or a colour that makes you feel your best can become a quiet reminder of the woman you’re working so hard to become. It’s not about expensive labels or following every trend. True style comes from authenticity, quality and wearing clothes that make you feel like yourself.

Over the years, I’ve met countless women through my work, and while every story is different, one thing remains the same. The most stylish women aren’t necessarily the ones with the biggest wardrobes; they’re the ones who wear their confidence with grace. They understand that getting dressed is not about impressing others it’s about stepping into the best version of themselves.

So the next time you stand in front of your wardrobe before an important  meeting, networking event or simply another busy day, remember that you’re not just choosing what to wear. You’re choosing how you want to feel.

Wear the woman you’re becoming. She deserves to be seen long before the rest of the world catches up.

Rebecca x Rebecca Rhoades’ craft is not about following trends - it is about designing garments that endure, that embody presence, and that speak without words. Visit her website to find out how Rebecca can help you.

storyLibrary.title: Mulch Ado About Nothing
storyLibrary.standfirst: The last time I was writing, I was sitting in a cool conservatory listening to the rain tapping on the roof of the conservatory.
storyLibrary.text:
The last time I was writing, I was sitting in a cool conservatory listening to the rain tapping on the roof of the conservatory. The skies were thick and grey and it really seemed as if, as has been the way in past years, that summer was already over.
How wrong I was! If meteorological reports are accurate, we are currently about to be plunged into the fourth heatwave of the year. This is excellent for sun-worshippers and those with a lot of laundry to dry, but it’s very hard work for allotment growers. I am slightly ashamed to admit that I had never actually measured the amount of water that I use in the garden, but I counted the number of trips I made with the watering can yesterday, and I was astonished that I’d used over 50 litres in the back garden alone. Being very much a Yorkshire girl at heart, I was horrified that I had ever contemplated using the hosepipe given that I’m on a meter. It really made me think about my water consumption, and the possibility of future hosepipe bans. The solution is of course, to make sure that my water butts are properly connected and running as efficiently as they can be so that nothing ever goes to waste.
Where I have seen a noticeable improvement to my profligate water consumption is that this year I mulched the garden very heavily. I invested in some bags of peat-free commercial mulch and covered the beds and dressed the tops of the pots. This was a worthwhile outlay, if only to alleviate my gardener’s anxiety - I was unable to water the garden for a couple of days as I was away, but on my return everything had survived. Not only that, but dressing the beds gives a uniform and tended-to look, so as the summer perennials begin to die back, there is still a neatness to everything.
From Thrift to Thriving
Over in my friend’s garden, where I have been helping to restore a previously unloved and neglected garden, I took inspiration from other local gardens. I noticed that in local gardens, jasmine and honeysuckle grow very well in the sheltered, slightly urban environment. These of course are superb varieties for those who enjoy an evening in the garden as they release their fragrance more potently after dusk. I also noticed that Agapanthus seems to thrive in the same environment. I seized the moment and located the pots that had shoved unceremoniously behind the shed that I suspected contained some Agapanthus rhizomes with nothing but a few green shoots, and I sunk them into the soil of the beds that I had cleared of discarded pots and garden rubbish. I really wasn’t sure if they would survive the shock, but with a combination of seaweed fertiliser, regular watering and a good dressing of mulch, they seem to have sprung to life! I am realistic and I know that we shall truly see the results next spring, but it is always rewarding to breathe new life into a once-forgotten plant.
Similarly, the Oxalis that we never knew existed in the fern garden seems to have its sights on world domination! This is possibly the happiest accident I’ve
ever known, but the deep purple shamrock-shaped leaves and delicate star-shaped lilac flowers complement the Hart’s Tongue fern superbly. I had absolutely no idea this plant was present until we embarked upon a strict regime of fertilising and watering. Whilst it has stopped flowering for now, the Clematis “Queen’s Nurse” provides a stunning backdrop against an otherwise drab fence and harmonises beautifully with the velvety purple Oxalis.
Get Ready for a Seasonal Wardrobe-change
My friends really did not appreciate me musing that Autumn is
approaching. We have past the Summer Solstice and the days are beginning to shorten. But I am not downbeat about the prospect at all because finally I can start on the cool season crops! I was not certain that I would see much success with seedlings during the recent hot weather, so I put a crop of Pak Choi seeds into the hydroponic propagator. I have them planted out now, in a raised planter with partial shade. This allows me to keep them cool enough to thrive and I don’t need to be concerned with watering more than once a day. Today’s task is to net them, as we have an awful lot of cabbages white butterflies who made a bee-line to lay their eggs on the undersides of the leaves. This will not stand, I’m afraid, and armed with a specialist egg-remover - a paintbrush - and some netting, I am determined to have my first crop within a week or two. Even as the summer flowers begin to fade, there is still ample time to get cool season crops such as lettuces, spinach and cavolo nero. Make kale while the sun shines!

storyLibrary.title: Each edition we bring to you a selection of books read and chosen by author Milly
storyLibrary.standfirst: Each edition we bring to you a selection of books read and chosen by author Milly Johnson.
storyLibrary.text:
Each edition we bring to you a selection of books read and chosen by author Milly Johnson. Milly is an author from Barnsley who has penned well over 20 books and is an ambassador for Yorkshire Businesswoman.

Summer at the French Bakery Jo Thomas Renegade Books, RRP £9.99 You can almost smell the croissants and bread baking in this joyful summer read. When Juliet buys an old watermill in France, her plans are sidelined when the local mayor asks her to consider reopening the village’s derelict boulangerie. But Juliet’s baking skills are limited, some of the locals are cranky and she has a rival determined to crush her. Everything seems pitted against her. But then the best dreams don’t come easy and with a little help from the charming Tabac owner, Juliet finds a zeal to reinstate the heart of the community. Romantic, lovely and (sort of) carb free!

Pet Sematary Stephen King Hodder, RRP £8.99 A little classic for anyone who hasn’t read it and by far, in my opinion, the best book Mr King has ever written. A family move into a community but when the daughter’s beloved cat is run over, a neighbour reluctantly tells the father that he could bury the cat in an ancient burial ground, which he does. And the cat returns to the family. But not quite the same as he used to be. And it’s not just pets that end up buried there and come back. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve read this.

The Lottery Winner Widows Club Penny Parkes Short Books, RRP - £10.99 When Paula loses her husband in a freak accident, she is amazed to find just a few days later she has won the lottery – on his ticket. Then she is approached by a group of glam fellow jackpot winners whose husbands mysteriously ‘died’ and they presume they have sniffed out someone in the same boat. It deals with a life changed by money and the inevitable chancers who come out of the woodwork wanting a slice. Thank goodness Paula has a new group of friends who understand just how to deal with them and negotiate all the changes. Elly Vine is the pseudonym of Lucy Vine and her trademark wicked humour is stamped all through this. It’s fresh, fun and feisty.

The Names Florence Knapp Phoenix , RRP £10.99 A book heralded as the best debut of the year.

It is 1987 and when Cora is set to register the birth of her son, it is expected that she follows tradition and name the baby after his father. But Cora is in two minds about calling him after generations of domineering men. Names are important she feels and can shape a destiny. So this is a book of three stories, three versions of a life where the baby is called Bear, Julian and Gordon after his father. At times it is a tough read, but always fascinating and will stay with you long after the last page. Hyped for good reason, I think!

storyLibrary.title: Summer Dining at Harvey Nichols
storyLibrary.standfirst: Harvey Nichols’ summer dining menu offers an impressive combination of quality, creativity, and value, with three courses accompanied by a Fever Tree Blush Spritz or Gin & Tonic for just £35 per person.
storyLibrary.text:
Harvey Nichols’ summer dining menu offers an impressive combination of quality, creativity, and value, with three courses accompanied by a Fever Tree Blush Spritz or Gin & Tonic for just £35 per person.  From the first course to the final spoonful of dessert, the experience felt thoughtfully curated and beautifully executed.
T
o start I chose the Whipped Feta, a vibrant and refreshing dish featuring mint, cucumber, oregano pressed tomatoes, sourdough crumb, and a rich red pepper reduction.  The flavours were perfectly balanced combining creamy, tangy, and herbaceous notes with a delightful crunch from the crumb.
My guest selected the Tandoori King Prawns (£3 supplement), served with cauliflower, coriander, samphire, and a zesty lime dressing.  The prawns were expertly cooked, carrying just the right amount of spice, while the accompanying vegetables and dressing brought freshness and complexity to the plate.
For the main course, I opted for the Chargrilled Flat Iron Steak (£7 supplement) Cooked exactly as requested, the steak was tender, flavourful, and complemented beautifully by a luxurious truffle macaroni and cheese croquette, roasted tenderstem broccoli, and a rich red wine jus.  The supplement felt entirely justified given the quality of the dish.
Meanwhile, my guest enjoyed the Tagliolini Pasta, a light yet satisfying combination of basil pesto, peas, broad beans, artichoke, lemon whipped ricotta, and pine nut and herb pangrattato.  Fresh, seasonal ingredients came together harmoniously, creating a dish that celebrated summer produce at it’s  finest.
Desserts maintained the high standard set by the earlier courses.  I chose the Strawberries, served with olive oil cake, basil jelly, mascarpone mousse, meringue, and strawberry sorbet.  This elegant summer dessert showcased strawberries at their best, with each component adding its own texture and flavour.  The olive oil cake was light and moist, the basil jelly introduced a subtle herbal freshness, while the mascarpone mousse added creamy richness.  Crisp meringue and vibrant strawberry sorbet completed a beautifully balanced plate that was both refreshing and indulgent.
My guest chose the Vanilla Crème Brulee, accompanied by dark chocolate ganache, cherries, amaretti biscuit, and lemon curd ice cream.  The dessert was beautifully balanced, combining creamy textures, crisp caramelisation, and bright citrus notes.
Both my guest and I then  sampled the Selection of Cheeses, served with crackers and chutney, offering a sophisticated and savoury contrast to the sweeter dessert and a fitting conclusion to the meal.
What truly elevated this experience was the presentation.  Every dish arrived looking immaculate, with exceptional attention to detail and a level of refinement that reflected Harvey Nichols reputation for quality dining.  Combined with attentive service and excellent value, this summer menu delivers a memorable dining experience that feels both indulgent and accessible.
Verdict:  Fabulous food, exceptional presentation, and remarkable value for money.  Harvey Nichols’ Summer Dining Menu is a
seasonal offering well worth seeking out.

storyLibrary.title: WIND IN THE HAIR, FLIES IN THE TEETH
storyLibrary.standfirst: Sensibly priced roadsters are a dying breed.
storyLibrary.text:
Sensibly priced roadsters are a dying breed. If you’re loaded, you can still have an openair experience with a properly engineered drop top…not something that’s had a tin opener to remove the roof.

Which is one reason why the Mazda MX-5 continues to be such a success…it follows the tried and tested formula of front engine, rear wheel drive, low seating position and a roof that can be lowered in seconds.

And it’s also affordable with a starting price of £28,605 (August ’26). Okay, if we’re being picky, you can get something like a Caterham Seven which starts at a similar price, but to say it’s a tad primitive is an understatement. If you option the ‘weather gear’ canvas roof, clambering in is like trying to get into a letterbox.

Back to the MX-5.

Choices within the MX-5 range are thin on the ground…you can have either the roadster with a canvas roof, or there’s a hard top model called the MX-5 RF (Retractable Fastback).

As for the trims, Prime-Line kicks off everything, then there’s Exclusive-Line (add (£2000), and fully stacked Homura which also gets a bigger engine (add a further £6000).

Entry level Prime-Line trim is only available with a 1.5 litre petrol 4-cylinder unit which develops 130 bhp and gives you a 0-60mph time of 8.3 seconds. Flat out you can manage 127 mph. Everything is fed to the rear wheels via one of the nicest 6-speed manual gearboxes you’re ever likely to find. 45.6mpg is the estimated economy.

Move up to Exclusive-Line and you can now stick with the 1.5 litre engine or opt for a 182bhp 2.0 litre unit. The 0-60mph sprint drops to 6.5 seconds. There are no automatic gearboxes available with either engine. If you go for Exclusive-Line with the bigger engine, add around £3k. Homura trim is only available with the 2.0 litre engine.

When did you last look out of your front door, spot that it isn’t raining, and go for a ride in your car…just for the shear fun of it?

Many of you will probably say…never.

When you have a Mazda MX-5, your life will change. It really is that good.

We love roadsters in the UK. If you work on a per-capita basis, we’re arguably the world’s no.1 market for open top motoring. It’s all down to our weather. If you’ve been to somewhere like Spain or Greece and hired an open top car, you’ll soon regret it because you fry. Here in Blighty, we tend to have sunny but cooler days.

It’s not only the enjoyment you get from driving with the roof down, it’s the way the MX-5 goes. 130bhp from the entry level 1.5 litre engine might not seem like very much power, but it’s sufficient for this lightweight car which only weighs a shade over one tonne.

In fact, it’s great to drive a car where you feel as though you’re doing everything. So many new cars nowadays are loaded with gadgets which either do something for you…or stop you from having a bit of fun. Granted, it’s all in the word of safety, but it means the driving experience can become staid and lifeless.

Not so with the Mazda MX-5. That’s one of the reasons why this little roadster is in the Guinness Book of Records for being the best-selling drop top of all time.

It’s decently equipped even in entry level Prime-Line, getting air con, powered windows, 7-inch driver display, heated seats, DAB radio, excellent audio system which has a couple of speakers built into the driver’s headrest, and a clear 8-inch central touchscreen which includes sat nav.

We’d probably spend the extra £2000 and go for Exclusive-Line because this now adds keyless entry, leather upholstery. LED headlights, and a powerful Bose audio system. It makes the car feel a tad more special.

Lowering and raising the roof is simple. Release a clip above the windscreen and throw the roof back until it clicks into the space behind the seats. Raising the roof is equally simple.

The Mazda MX-5 offers traditional, British, open top driving without too many compromises. It harks back to the days of simple, seat of the pants driving. It’s lively, decently equipped and is something of a bargain. Mazda will launch an updated Mk5 at some point. We hope they change…nothing.
